Title: John Ternus to lead Apple into the age of AI
Article:
SAN FRANCISCO, (United States):
John Ternus takes over as Apple's chief executive on Tuesday, inheriting a company that towers over the smartphone market but trails its rivals in artificial intelligence.
One of his biggest challenges will be balancing the company's dependence on China while parrying acute political pressure from the White House.
The handover ends Tim Cook's 15-year run, replacing the operations specialist who built Apple's supply chain with the engineer who built its hardware.
Ternus, 51, joined Apple's design team in 2001 and worked his way up to senior vice president of hardware engineering, reporting to Cook.
He leads the engineering teams behind Apple's entire product lineup, including the iPhones that generate most of the company's revenue.
He gets barely a week to settle in, with Apple holding its annual iPhone event on September 9, where it is expected to unveil its first foldable handset.
"Tim Cook left the house in phenomenal order," said Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at investment firm Yorkville Ives & Co.
"But now it's about Ternus defining the AI chapter."
Ives expects the new chief executive to lean into what he knows.
"There's no reason to fix what's already working," he said, predicting Ternus will concentrate on hardware innovation while leaving Cook's supply chain intact.
Some analysts had argued software chief Craig Federighi was the more logical pick for a company scrambling to catch up on AI.
Carolina Milanesi, an analyst at Creative Strategies, said that misreads how consumers actually adopt technology.
"Consumers are still buying hardware first, and it's going to be like that for a long time," she said.
"You're not going to discover the value of AI if you're not interested in the hardware."
Ternus earned a bachelor's degree in mechanical engineering from the University of Pennsylvania and worked as an engineer at Virtual Research Systems before joining Apple.
Inside the company he is credited with driving a push to make products more durable, reliable and resilient, and with design work that cut their carbon footprint.
The harder question is what kind of leader he becomes.
"Even people that know him now don't know him as a CEO," Milanesi said.
"You might know him as the head of engineering, but once you're CEO, things change. Your responsibility is bigger, your power is bigger. You're dancing a different kind of dance."
- 'Learn on the job' -
Nowhere is that gap wider than in the geopolitical role Cook excelled at, courting both Beijing and Donald Trump's White House to protect a supply chain that runs largely through China.
Apple's manufacturing operation is among the most complex in corporate history, a web of hundreds of suppliers and assembly lines that Cook painstakingly built over decades.
Cook in recent years began shifting some of the work elsewhere — iPhone assembly to India, other production to Vietnam — but the diversification has been gradual with China, one of Apple's biggest consumer markets, still anchoring the system.
Complicating matters, Trump has repeatedly demanded Apple build iPhones on American soil, threatening tariffs on those made overseas.
Cook avoided the heaviest blows of Trump's trade war by cultivating the president directly, making US investment commitments and political donations — all while also keeping Beijing onside.
The tricky political terrain will be new for Ternus.
"He knows Apple Park like the back of his pocket in terms of hardware," Ives said of Ternus.
"But on the global stage — that's probably one of the biggest areas where he's going to have to learn on the job."
Cook is not going far. He becomes executive chairman of Apple's board on the same day, with a mandate the company has said includes engaging policymakers around the world.
"That was really clever," said Milanesi, arguing the arrangement frees Ternus from a role Cook has handled alone for years.
The September 9 iPhone event will be the first public measure of the handover.
A foldable iPhone would be the most significant redesign in years, and Ternus will be its face — eight days into the job.
"This is a moment that they created for him," Milanesi said. — AFP

Title: Ong Kian Ming quits DAP, to help KJ in GE16
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: Former Bangi member of parliament Dr Ong Kian Ming has announced his resignation from DAP.
The former international trade and industry deputy minister said that while he would no longer be an active politician, he would continue serving the nation alongside like-minded people.
Ong said he would help former health minister Khairy Jamaluddin in his 16th General Election (GE16) campaign.
In a Facebook post addressed to DAP secretary-general Anthony Loke, Ong announced that his resignation takes effect today.
"I am grateful for the opportunity to contribute to the party and country in various ways since joining in 2012, as the MP for Serdang (2013 to 2018) and Bangi (2018 to 2022), deputy international trade and industry minister (2018 to 2020), an appointed Central Executive Committee member (2019 to 2022), and an elected DAP Selangor committee member (2018 to 2024)."
He thanked former Petaling Jaya Utara MP Tony Pua for inviting him to join DAP and guiding him on how best to serve the party and nation over the past 14 years.
"I am also grateful to Lim Guan Eng for giving me the opportunity to be nominated for the Serdang and Bangi parliamentary seats, and as a deputy minister during his tenure as DAP secretary-general.
"It was an honour to work with DAP members and leaders in Serdang and Bangi during my term as an MP from 2013 to 2022, serving the constituents and residents as their elected representative," he said.
Ong said he had no plans to join any other political party in the near future, nor did he intend to contest as a candidate in GE16.

Title: Sarawak air quality worsens, 4 areas record hazardous API readings
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: Air quality in Sarawak worsened today, with four locations recording hazardous readings and three others entering the "very unhealthy" category as of 8.45am on National Day.
Of the 68 air quality monitoring stations nationwide, one recorded good air quality, 45 were in the moderate range and 21 recorded readings ranging from unhealthy to hazardous, while no reading was available for Temerloh in Perak.
According to the Department of Environment's Air Pollutant Index Management System (APIMS), the Serian police headquarters recorded the country's highest Air Pollutant Index (API) reading at 476, up from 436 at 5.45pm yesterday.
Sri Aman's reading surged from 260 to 326, pushing it from the very unhealthy category into the hazardous range.
Samarahan and Kuching remained hazardous, although their readings eased slightly from 337 to 330 and 321 to 317, respectively.
Mukah recorded a sharp increase from 185 to 267, moving from unhealthy to very unhealthy.
Sibu also entered the very unhealthy category after its reading rose from 195 to 219, while Sarikei remained in the same category as its reading increased slightly from 210 to 214.
Fourteen stations recorded unhealthy readings, including Limbang (159), Miri (170), ILP Miri (168), Bintulu (162), Kapit (164) and Samalaju (181) in Sarawak.
The other stations included Seberang Jaya (155), Seberang Perai (154) and Minden (152) in Penang; Politeknik Kota Kinabalu (116) and Tawau (152) in Sabah; Sungai Petani in Kedah (157); Taiping in Perak (141); and Labuan (156).
An API reading of between zero and 50 is categorised as good, 51 to 100 as moderate, 101 to 200 as unhealthy, 201 to 300 as very unhealthy, and above 300 as hazardous.

Title: Media Prima contingent joins National Day parade in Putrajaya
Article:
PUTRAJAYA: Media Prima Bhd (MPB), Malaysia's largest integrated media group, added colour to the 2026 National Day celebrations by taking part in the parade to foster patriotism and love for the country.
Taking part under the Digital Connectivity Cluster, 17 employees from various departments marched along the main route at Dataran Putrajaya here alongside participants from the country's leading media and telecommunications companies.
The MPB contingent was led by Khairul Affandi Azlan, with each participant carrying and waving the Jalur Gemilang, while several others held banners bearing the MPB logo.
Besides MPB, the parade group included other local broadcasters and telecommunications organisations, including the Malaysian Communications and Multimedia Commission (MCMC), Radio Television Malaysia (RTM), Astro and CelcomDigi Bhd.
The group was among 366 participants under the Economy Contingent.
This year's celebration involves 10,819 participants, 77 contingents, 22 marching bands, 328 land and air assets, 112 animals in service and 11 decorated floats, with the event being broadcast live and followed by millions of Malaysians on television and social media platforms.
They represent various government agencies, security forces, government-linked companies (GLCs) and the private sector.

Title: National Day celebrations kick off with arrival of King and Queen [WATCH]
Article:
PUTRAJAYA: The 2026 National Day celebration procession officially began following the arrival of His Majesty Sultan Ibrahim, King of Malaysia, and Her Majesty Raja Zarith Sofiah, Queen of Malaysia.
Their Majesties arrived at 8am and were received by Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim.
Their Majesties' arrival was also greeted with a Royal Salute and the national anthem, Negaraku.
Sultan Ibrahim then inspected the parade and received the Royal Salute from the Main Guard of Honour, comprising four officers and 103 personnel from the First Battalion, Royal Malay Regiment, based at Perdana Camp in Sungai Besi.
This was followed by a flypast involving five helicopters adorned with the Jalur Gemilang, as well as the flags of the armed forces, army, Royal Malaysian Navy and Royal Malaysian Air Force, over the skies of Putrajaya.
Negaraku was played once again as the Jalur Gemilang was hoisted, accompanied by a 14-gun salute fired by the 41st Battery of the Royal Artillery Regiment (Ceremonial).
The event continued with the recitation of the Rukun Negara pledge by Fire and Rescue Department deputy commissioner Datuk Abdul Razak Muda, joined by 69 personnel from the Fire and Rescue Department and sign language interpreter Nur Alyanatasha.

Title: Death toll from Nepal, Tibet floods, landslides rises to 804, nearly 3,300 remain missing
Article:
DEVIGHAT, (Nepal): The death toll from devastating flash floods and landslides in Nepal and China's Tibet region has climbed to 804, while nearly 3,300 people remain missing, Anadolu Ajansi reported, citing  the latest figures released by authorities and local media on Sunday.
In Nepal, police authorities said they have recovered 788 bodies from floods-hit areas, whereas, 2,742 people remain missing, including hundreds of foreign nationals. Chinese authorities reported 16 deaths and 546 people missing in Tibet.
Search and rescue operations are underway for 2,498 people who remain missing, including 933 workers at hydropower projects, 589 foreign nationals, 127 Nepalis travelling with foreign tourists, and residents from several affected districts, local sources reported.
Nearly 20,000 security personnel have rescued 8,186 people, while helicopter operations evacuated 279 hydropower workers and 227 foreign nationals to safety.
Relief operations are underway, with food and essential supplies being delivered, medical teams deployed, and government cash aid distributed, Nepal News reported.
The disaster struck the China-Nepal border region on Wednesday when a sudden glacial collapse sent a powerful surge of water and debris through Himalayan valleys, destroying villages and severely damaging major infrastructure.
The scale of the devastation has left families desperately searching for loved ones who remain missing.
Authorities are racing to preserve evidence and find space for the dead as hospital mortuaries reach capacity and recovered remains begin to decompose.
The US announced more than US$3.6 million (RM14.49 million) in humanitarian assistance for flood-hit Nepal on Saturday, including emergency food aid for up to 10,000 affected households.
Deputy Inspector General Abi Narayan Kafle, the Nepal Police spokesperson, told the Kathmandu Post that the distance over which bodies had been carried by floodwaters had made identification particularly difficult.
Many recovered bodies "were found as mutilated, partial or severed remains, making visual identification extraordinarily difficult," Kafle said.
"Many remains were buried under thick mud and water for two to three days."
Search and rescue operations have been complicated by the region's rugged terrain, steep mountains, and narrow gorges.
Nepal has sought specialised assistance for tunnel rescues, survivor-detection technology, forensic and DNA analysis, as well as equipment to preserve recovered bodies.
An 11-member tunnel rescue reconnaissance team from India has already arrived to support the operation.
Authorities are also closely monitoring a newly formed lake in the Himalayas that had raised fears of another flood.
Chinese officials said the lake had significantly shrunk and was now "essentially drained" after releasing its water naturally, easing concerns of an immediate new surge. — BERNAMA

Title: Patriotism starts with the choices we make
Article:
BEYOND flying the Jalur Gemilang and attending Merdeka parades, patriotism can also be expressed through everyday consumer choices.
These choices can support local entrepreneurs, safeguard jobs and boost the domestic economy.
This spirit underpins "Jom Malaysia: Jom Beli Produk Malaysia", a government-led movement aimed at encouraging Malaysians to recognise, support and take pride in home-grown products and services.
Encouraging people to buy local is not a new concept.Launched in 1984, the 'Kempen Beli Barangan  Malaysia' (KBBM) has long promoted homegrown goods.
However, four decades later, consumer behaviour has changed dramatically, with shoppers turning to smartphones, e-commerce platforms and social media to compare prices, quality and reviews.
To keep pace with changing consumer habits, Domestic Trade and Cost of Living Minister Datuk Armizan Mohd Ali launched the evolved Jom Malaysia initiative during the Jom Malaysia Festival at Pasar Seni on June 27.
Far from being a cosmetic rebranding, the initiative aims to transform the effort into a national movement that supports local brands and helps them  expand into international markets.
While the government provides the framework, building a sustainable ecosystem requires broad participation.
Entrepreneurs must maintain and improve quality, retailers need to give greater prominence to local goods, digital platforms can broaden market reach and consumers must exercise their purchasing power.
Local products face stiff competition from cheaper imports, but Malaysian consumers are becoming increasingly discerning, assessing goods based on design, innovation, quality and overall value.
[[nid:1522442]]
At the same time, many domestic brands have significantly improved their offerings, with several earning international recognition and successfully entering overseas markets.
The core objective of Jom Malaysia is, therefore, not for consumers to buy local simply out of obligation or patriotic sentiment. Instead, Malaysian products should become the preferred choice because they offer competitive quality, value and innovation.
This distinction is important as the campaign seeks to build lasting consumer confidence rather than rely solely on patriotic appeals.
Over the next decade, the goal is to make choosing home-grown brands a natural part of everyday life.
When Malaysian brands succeed globally, their achievements can boost  national confidence while reinforcing an economic ecosystem supported by local workers, manufacturers, entrepreneurs and technology providers.
A robust domestic market can also enable local enterprises to expand, create jobs, invest in innovation and eventually compete more effectively in international markets.
The benefits of supporting local businesses can, therefore, extend beyond individual purchases, contributing to a stronger and more resilient domestic economy.
Ultimately, Jom Malaysia is about building confidence in Malaysian capabilities and giving deeper meaning to patriotism.
The initiative encourages Malaysians to see their purchasing decisions as one way of contributing to the country's economic future.
Patriotism does not have to be expressed only through the Jalur Gemilang, Merdeka celebrations or national ceremonies.
It can also begin with a simple choice - to buy Malaysian  products because we believe in what Malaysians can create, produce and achieve.
The aspiration is simple: Jom Beli Produk Malaysia.

Title: Negri Sembilan sets sights on 2,405 projects by 2040
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: Negri Sembilan is targeting more than an eight-fold increase in the number of investment projects in the state by 2040, with vast tracts of undeveloped land identified as a key advantage in attracting future investment.
Menteri Besar Datuk Ismail Lasim said the state had a built-up area of only about 12.55 per cent, leaving significant room for strategic development as it positions itself for its next phase of economic growth.
"The increase in economic competitiveness is also reflected in the targeted growth in the number of investment projects in Negri Sembilan, from 295 projects worth RM19.1 billion in 2025 to 2,405 projects by 2040."
Ismail said the target would be supported by 14 investment sector focus areas, comprising nine development parcels within the Malaysia Vision Valley (MVV) area and five flagships outside MVV.
"The state's relatively low level of development means Negri Sembilan still has substantial capacity to accommodate industrial expansion, new townships, as well as domestic and foreign investments.
[[nid:1522437]]
"This reflects the state's considerable development capacity and competitiveness to support economic growth, the expansion of industrial activities, the development of new cities and the entry of domestic and foreign investments in the future."
The development push is expected to significantly expand the state's economy, with its gross domestic product (GDP) valued at RM57.01 billion last year and projected to reach RM109.12 billion by 2040.
Ismail said the growth would be driven by high-impact projects in the Seremban Economic Development Zone and Port Dickson under MVV 2.0, which are expected to serve as catalysts for industrial development, investment and land use.
At the same time, the state is looking beyond industrial development, with a proposed agricultural promotion zone covering Tampin, Jempol, Rembau and Kuala Pilah expected to serve as a catalyst for agricultural activities.
Jelebu, meanwhile, will see greater emphasis on biodiversity and ecotourism.
Ismail said the state's population was also projected to increase from 1.2 million in 2025 to 1.6 million by 2040, providing a larger population and workforce to support the planned development.
However, he said growth must not come at the expense of balanced development or the environment.
"We do not want development to be concentrated in certain areas alone. Instead, development must be felt inclusively across all districts, including rural areas," he said.
[[nid:1522436]]
Ismail said the state administration would also incorporate digitalisation and new technologies, including artificial intelligence, into development management and government delivery systems.
This, he said, would enable decisions to be made more efficiently, accurately and responsively while keeping the state aligned with its carbon-neutral targets.
"The state's development strategy would ultimately be measured by its impact on people's lives, including the creation of jobs, quality housing, better public amenities, efficient transportation and a safe and conducive environment."
He added that the administration's approach would be guided by three core principles - stability, progress and prosperity - with development expected to create quality investments, high-value employment and opportunities across the state rather than being concentrated in a single area.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Crowds gather for 69th National Day celebrations in Putrajaya
Article:
PUTRAJAYA: Families arrived at Dataran Putrajaya before dawn, staking out spots along the parade route hours before the 69th National Day celebration began.
Omar Muhammad said he made the trip with more than 10 family members from Semenyih, leaving home at around 3.30am and arriving shortly after 4am.
He wore a batik shirt featuring the Malaysian flag to showcase his patriotism.
"I heard the Johor Military Forces are taking part this year, so I want to see them.
"This year is the first time they're joining. Because we're from Mersing, Johor, we have to support Johor," he said.
Sivanessan Murthi, who travelled from Klang with his family, said they left home at 3am and reached the venue by bus at around 4am after being dropped off at the Putrajaya International Convention Centre (PICC).
"I've been following the news, and they said people started gathering since last night.
"So we considered ourselves quite late," he said, adding that his family hoped to make the trip an annual tradition after starting last year.
He said the group of six were most looking forward to seeing military vehicles in the parade, with one member hoping to relive her experience from national service.
College student Jarrel Sistarted his journey as early as 3.30am via an e-hailing ride, enduring an hour-long commute marked by minor traffic jams and road accidents along the route.
Marking his second time attending the parade, the Sarawakian said he was most looking forward to viewing the armed forces contingents during the parade.
"I'm really looking forward to the armed forces personnel and seeing them carry their equipment. Their presence during the march is impressive," he said.
Zara Abdullah, who lives in Putrajaya, said this was her first time attending the celebration in person after previously only watching broadcasts on television.
"It feels fun, right? It's heartening because of the crowd's spirit to celebrate our Independence Day," she said.
Policemen were stationed around the venue to guard the area and ensure crowd control ran smoothly.
Carrying the theme "Malaysia Madani: Kesejahteraan Dinikmati", this year's National Day celebration features programmes aimed at fostering patriotism while highlighting Malaysia's history, identity and spirit of independence.
The event, which begins at 8am, will feature 10,819 participants across 76 contingents, supported by 22 marching bands, 11 floats, 328 land, naval and air assets, 112 working animals and 22 electric vehicle assets.

Title: Dear Malaysia
Article:
SELAMAT Hari Kebangsaan and Selamat Hari Malaysia, my dear fellow Malaysians.
For the past five years, I have shared my thoughts with you around National Day. Each year, I reflected on the many challenges facing our beloved nation; our economy, education, corruption, political reforms, climate change, artificial intelligence and the rapidly changing world around us.
These challenges remain relevant and important. This year, I like to speak about something even more fundamental — who we are as a people.
I often ask myself a simple question. What do all Malaysians have in common?
Before we are Malays, Chinese, Indians, Ibans, Kadazans, Orang Asli or Eurasian and before we belong to different political parties or hold different opinions — who are we?
We are all sons and daughters of Malaysia. Many of us become husbands and wives. Many become mothers and fathers. We celebrate when our children succeed. We lose sleep when they struggle. We worry when our parents grow old. We grieve when those we love leave us. We hope that the next generation will enjoy a better life than we did.
When we strip away everything else, we discover something beautiful and enlightening. We are far more alike than we are different.
I grew up in a small town called Pusing in Perak. My closest childhood friends were Malays, Chinese and Indians. We played sports together. We swam in the old mining pools and rivers together. We often visited and slept over in each othersʼ homes.
I honestly cannot remember asking anyone what race they were before deciding whether they could be my friend. Children have a remarkable gift. They see people before they see labels. Perhaps somewhere along the journey of adulthood, we lose a little of that wisdom.
Every child born into this world is a gift to humankind. None of us had the privilege to choose the colour of our skin and where we were born. Faith is indeed a deeply personal matter. None of us chose our first language and the family into which we entered this world.
Every one of us can decide, every single day, what kind of Malaysian we want to become. That choice has always been ours. And it will always be.
Whatever our faith may be, all religions teach us the same fundamental truth and wisdom, that every human life possesses dignity. Whatever our faith, surely none teaches us to despise another human being because of race or religion.
At Sunway, I always strive to ensure we are "colour-blind, passport-blind and religion-blind".
As a nation of diverse cultures and creeds, our diversity is indeed a strength to be cherished.
We must deepen our resolve to build a country where all may live with dignity and a true sense of belonging.
Hatred is learnt. Respect can also be learnt. Division is cultivated. Unity can also be cultivated. The question before us is not whether Malaysia can become a more united nation. The question is whether each of us is prepared to become a more generous Malaysian.
Because nations do not become better by themselves. People do.
Throughout history, there have always been those who unite people. Unfortunately, there are also those who sought to divide us.
Division is easy. It takes little effort to convince one community to fear another. It takes far greater courage to build trust. Often times, there is a heavy price to pay for doing what is right and just.
We must remain steadfast in our convictions to uphold the ideals that bind us as a nation.
[[nid:1522421]]
Every generation is eventually remembered by the bridges it built, or the walls it left behind. Our generation will be no different.
Sometimes I wonder how much further Malaysia might already have progressed if we devoted the same energy to solving our common problems as we have spent fighting and arguing over our differences.
Imagine if we competed to build better schools instead of sharper slogans, if we invested more in educating our children than in insulting one another.
Imagine if we became known not for the loudest voices, but for the wisest ideas on how to build a better nation.
When I was a young boy, poverty shaped my life. It taught me that education is the most powerful pathway out of hardship and misery towards a life of dignity. That conviction never left me.
The success of my business career has given me the privilege to set up the Jeffrey Cheah Foundation to make quality education accessible to as many young Malaysians as possible, regardless of race and background.
This is why I transferred, in perpetuity, my entire equity in the Sunway Education Group (Sunway International Schools, Sunway Colleges and Sunway University) to the Jeffrey Cheah Foundation in a not-for-profit structure.
The foundation no longer belongs to me nor my family. It belongs to Malaysia for the benefit of present and future generations of Malaysians.
More than RM4 billion has been gifted and endowed in perpetuity through the foundation, with over RM1.05 billion in scholarships and grants awarded to date.
Every scholarship awarded is not simply another student entering college or university. It is a family lifted out of the vicious cycle of poverty and misery. A dream restored. A future rewritten. That, to me, is nation-building.
Yet governments alone cannot build a great nation. Businesses, schools, religious organisations and parents cannot do it alone.
Every citizen has a part to play.
A better Malaysia is not something we inherit. It is something we build, together.
The world will not wait for us. Artificial Intelligence is transforming how we live, learn and work. Climate change is reshaping our future. Our neighbours and other countries around the world are investing heavily in innovation, education and human capital.
While the world races forward, Malaysia cannot afford to be left behind and be distracted by fear, suspicion and endless division. Our children deserve better than that. They deserve a nation confident enough to compete with the rest of the world.
Whether Malaysia remains competitive regionally or globally is really a question of how well prepared our next generation is for that competition.
Our duty as fathers, mothers and grandparents is to prepare our next generation to meet this very fierce, intensive and relentless competition.
In spite of all the challenges before us, I remain hopeful. Whenever I meet young Malaysians, I am encouraged by their curiosity, creativity, compassion and confidence.
Perhaps they will succeed where previous generations, including mine, have sometimes fallen short. Perhaps they will finally build the Malaysia we have always dreamed of. I sincerely believe they can and pray they will succeed.
Every one of us will leave this world one day. People are unlikely to remember which political party we supported. They will probably not remember the arguments we fought and debated on social media.
But they will remember whether we left Malaysia in a better state than we found it.
Kinder, fairer, more united, more stable and more hopeful. That, to me, is the true meaning of patriotism. Not merely loving our country for what it is today, but loving it enough to help it become the Malaysia that we can all be proud of.
This is our home and shared inheritance. This is our responsibility and shared destiny.
Let us build bridges strong enough for the next generation to cross. Let us foster a more stable, just, inclusive and sustainable future for our beloved country.
Because the Malaysia we leave behind is the Malaysia our children will inherit.
Together, with conviction, let us build a nation worthy of them. We are all in this together and may we all be blessed, always. Selamat Hari Kebangsaan. Selamat Hari Malaysia.
Tan Sri Dr Jeffrey Cheah
A Fellow Malaysian
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Fine weather greets 69th National Day celebrations in Putrajaya
Article:
PUTRAJAYA: Fine weather accompanied the 2026 National Day celebrations at Dataran Putrajaya this morning.
Based on the Malaysian Air Pollutant Index Management System (APIMS) portal, the Air Pollutant Index (API) reading in Putrajaya stood at 79 as of 7am.
The reading was categorised as moderate, but air quality remained under control and did not affect the smooth running of the country's 69th National Day celebrations.
Checks found that visibility was good, allowing the parade, procession and air show to proceed as scheduled.
Malaysians from all walks of life began filling the area around Dataran Putrajaya as early as 4am to witness the celebrations.

Title: National Day: Early birds flock to Dataran Putrajaya for prime spots, best shots
Article:
PUTRAJAYA: Eager to witness the 69th National Day celebration up close, members of the public began gathering at Dataran Putrajaya as early as yesterday evening, with some camping overnight to secure prime viewing spots along the parade route.
For Mock Wei Qi, 23, and his friends, their shared passion for photography and cinematography brought them to the venue at 11pm yesterday in search of the perfect spot to capture creative and cinematic footage showcasing Malaysia's unique features.
"We are looking for the best spots to capture creative and cinematic views. We want to show the world how special our country is," he told Bernama.
The freelance photographer said he saw the National Day celebration as a perfect opportunity to put his skills to the test while capturing memorable moments through his lens.
Meanwhile, a married couple, who wished to be known only as As and Adib, reached the venue with their children as early as 5pm yesterday, hoping to get a better view this year after being late last year and having to watch the celebration from afar.
"Last year, we arrived late and ended up quite far from the main area. This time, we decided to come early to get a spot closer to the celebration and enjoy a better view," said Adib.
For Ahmad Azri Onn, 55, who attended with his wife and three children aged between 10 and 15, spending the night at the venue turned the wait for the celebration into a fun 'camping experience' for the family.
Having arrived at about 5.30pm yesterday, Ahmad Azri said his family was thrilled to get a good viewing spot, giving the children a chance to experience the National Day celebration firsthand during the school holidays.
"The weather was not a problem for us. The drizzle yesterday helped a bit with the heat, and the children were comfortable," he said.
Dataran Putrajaya began filling up this morning as people gathered to witness the 69th National Day celebration, themed "Malaysia Madani: Kesejahteraan Dinikmati", which is scheduled to begin at 8am.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: 'Proud and excited': RMAF chief leads National Day flypast [WATCH]
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: "Subang Tower, this is Kris Mas, proceeding out to taxiway Yankee to Runway 33 for takeoff."
General Tan Sri Muhamad Norazlan Aris draws a lungful of oxygen through his Ulmer O2 mask and slips into the familiar cadence of a fighter pilot.
Today, the Royal Malaysian Air Force chief traded his customary blue digital camouflage battle dress uniform (BDU) for the PPK-3P-120M flight suit, Mk46SV survival vest and Gallet LA100 flight helmet as he prepares to lead the National Day flypast over Putrajaya.
The feeling, he said, was still one of pride and excitement, tempered by a comfortable sense of familiarity.
For the second consecutive year, Norazlan is piloting the Sukhoi Su-30MKM, leading a formation of three other Su-30MKMs, four F/A-18D Hornets and two BAE Systems Hawks over the administrative capital for Malaysia's 69th National Day celebrations.
"I feel proud and excited. More importantly, I see it as a responsibility to continue defending the country," he said.
For Norazlan, whose call sign is "Giro", flying one of the RMAF's frontline fighters means more than simply taking to the skies.
It is about leading from the front and reflects the responsibility he carries as service chief — ensuring Malaysia's airspace remains secure.
"Our main responsibility is to ensure the country's airspace is always safe and remains under our control.
"Our readiness must be high. We must have capable assets, an effective defence system, as well as trained and professional personnel," he said.
LEADING FROM THE COCKPIT
Norazlan's decision to remain "current" reflects his approach to leadership.
Despite holding the RMAF's highest appointment, he maintains a direct connection with its operational environment — leading not only from the command centre, but also from the cockpit.
His message to younger officers is simple: never stop learning and never become complacent.
"Improve your skills and do not be easily satisfied. Maintain your fighting spirit and always be ready to defend the homeland," he said.
Norazlan added that being an effective military aviator went beyond mastering an aircraft.
Rapid technological advances, he said, were among the greatest challenges in preparing the next generation of RMAF pilots.
"Young pilots must master new technologies while maintaining the discipline, courage and patriotism expected of those entrusted with defending the country.
"We want to produce pilots who are not only capable of flying aircraft, but who also possess strong character and a deep sense of responsibility towards the nation," he said.
'A TRUST THAT MUST BE DEFENDED'
That sense of duty is also central to Norazlan's understanding of Merdeka.
For him, independence is more than the freedom to celebrate Malaysia's sovereignty; it is the freedom to shape the nation's future — and, above all, the resolve and ability to defend it.
"For me, Merdeka means that we are free to determine our own future and are capable of defending Malaysia's sovereignty and dignity," he said.
He urged young Malaysians to value that freedom by pursuing knowledge, strengthening their capabilities and contributing to the nation.
"Love the country not only through words, but through contributions and actions," he said.
"The service must remain ready, continuously improve its capabilities and ensure its personnel maintain the highest professional standards," he said.
And as Norazlan works through his takeoff checklist and prepares to push the twin throttles of the Lyulka Saturn AL-31FP augmented turbofans past the detent and into full burner, the sight of the RMAF chief at the controls represents far more than a dramatic opening to the Merdeka flypast.
It is a statement of leadership and a demonstration of readiness.
More importantly, it is a reminder that sovereignty is not merely declared — it must be protected, every day and in every domain.
Because, as Norazlan puts it, "Independence is not just something to be celebrated, but a trust that must be defended."

Title: Making a living in a shadow of history
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: At the ticketing entrance of Stadium Merdeka, Rusilawati Borhan, better known as Cik Comel, spent Ramadan selling kuih and nasi lemak as the historic landmark came alive again.
For her, returning to the stadium where Tunku Abdul Rahman proclaimed Merdeka on Aug 31, 1957 was more than finding a place to set up a stall.
It became a place where she and her vendors, including elderly women and single mothers, could sell their kuih, earn a livelihood and build a sense of community.
MORE THAN A TRADING SPOT
Cik Comel, 54, said setting up her stall at the stadium brought back memories of visiting the landmark with her husband when they were younger.
"I opened my stall right at the stadium's ticketing entrance. I used to come here with my husband when we were younger, riding   our motorcycle around the area.
"When I first came back to the stadium, I was amazed by the restoration. It is now a wonderful and safe place for people to exercise, relax, jog and spend time. I am very happy," she said.
But the Ramadan bazaar became more than a personal trip down memory lane.
The mother of two did not miss a single day, despite a quiet start.
"On the first day, I was the only one there. People were asking, 'Is there anyone here?' But by the third day, people started coming. Praise be to God, the response was good. "It helped many
asnaf
, single mothers and retirees."
The bazaar eventually drew large crowds, providing an income not only for Cik Comel but also for the women whose food she sold.
She works with about 18 suppliers, although 10 to 12 typically deliver their products on any given day. Many are single mothers, senior citizens, women with large families and members of the asnaf community.
Among them is a 72-year-old woman who makes
cekodok pisang
and marble cake, while another, aged 69, makes
lepat pisang
and
lepat ubi
.
For Cik Comel, selling their food is not about making a large profit. Her commission can be as little as 10 or 20 sen.
"Some people ask, 'Is there really a 10-sen commission?' Yes, there is. Even if I make RM70 a day, I am grateful.
"If there are more orders, there is more money, and I would be happier," she said.
Seeing her suppliers earn an income, she said, was more rewarding than the modest commissions she received.
"If the women who send me their food are happy, I am even happier because we can help them.
"There are single mothers and even retirees who are still looking for ways to earn money. It helps them very much," she said.
OPPORTUNITIES ABOUND
The opportunities around Stadium Merdeka and the wider Merdeka 118 precinct  also extend beyond Ramadan.
Cik Comel said she would  trade at events whenever she was offered an affordable or free space, regardless of the expected crowd.
"If there is an event, I will go. I do not think about whether there will be sales or many people.
"I will bring the food there and sell. Praise be to God, the response has been good. Whenever Stadium Merdeka holds an event, many people come," she said.
She has since sold at various events around the area, including family programmes and events featuring performers.
LIVELIHOOD BORN FROM
HARDSHIP
Cik Comel's journey as a trader began long before she set up at Stadium Merdeka.
She first turned to Baitulmal for help after her husband was injured in a hit-and-run motorcycle accident 14 years ago, leaving him unable to do heavy work.
"He is still being monitored and undergoing treatment."
With her husband unable to work, Cik Comel became the family's  breadwinner.
She  wakes about 2am to prepare roti jala and nasi lemak before starting work  at 6.15am and continuing until 1pm.
Despite the long hours and modest returns, she remains determined to keep going and wants other women facing hardship to believe they can do the same.
"Do not say 'no' to earning a living. We can  break out of our struggles to earn money and help our families.
"If we cannot go out, we can sell from home.  Now, we can take orders online. We have to be strong and help ourselves get back on our feet."

Title: Restoring the home of Merdeka
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR:   Stadium Merdeka, where Tunku Abdul Rahman proclaimed independence in 1957, is no longer a monument frozen in time.
Restored to closely resemble its 1957 appearance, the stadium is now a living history book, allowing a new generation to step into the setting where the nation was born.
The timber-strip seats line the terraces. The original colour scheme has returned.
Even features that disappeared over the decades have been painstakingly recreated, bringing the stadium closer to is 1957 appearance, when  Tunku Abdul Rahman Putra Al-Haj declared "Merdeka" seven times.
When it reopened to the public on Aug 17, 2024, after  a major restoration that began in 2017 and sought to return the landmark to its  1957 appearance, the task was never simply about repairing an old stadium.
It was about preserving the history and memories embedded within its walls while understanding what should  be retained, removed or reconstructed.
For PNB Merdeka Ventures, the custodian of Stadium Merdeka, the challenge was to preserve  its past without turning it into a relic.
[[nid:1522495]]
PNB Merdeka Ventures chief executive officer Datuk Izwan Hasli Mohd Ibrahim said the restoration was guided by a simple challenge, preserving the stadium's historical and architectural significance while keeping  it  relevant to Kuala Lumpur today.
"When we planned to restore Stadium Merdeka, our priority was to bring it back as closely as possible to its  1957 form, while ensuring that it could continue to serve a purpose today.
"We wanted to preserve what made the stadium historically and architecturally significant.
"We also wanted Malaysians to be able to come back to this historic place, stand on the same grounds where independence was proclaimed and experience that history for themselves," he told the
New Straits Times
.
WHEN LESS IS MORE
Beneath the restored colours and timber seats lay a far more complicated problem.
Over the decades, Stadium Merdeka had undergone several modifications, including the addition of reinforced concrete upper terraces, which  increased the load on the original structure.
"When the stadium was  built in 1957, it had a capacity of 20,000. Over time, we kept adding capacity and it became 40,000.
"But when the team debated it, we said heritage was more important. So we removed the additions and restored it to its 1957 form.
"It was a big decision because you are effectively reducing the seats from 40,000 to 20,000, but this was built for heritage," he said.
The work was complicated by the fact that the team was not starting from scratch.
[[nid:1522494]]
"One of the biggest challenges is that you are working with a structure that has gone through decades of change.
"Unlike constructing a new building, you are not starting with a blank sheet of paper."
Modern requirements also had to be incorporated without compromising the stadium's historic character.
"During the restoration, a lift was incorporated to provide  access from the ground floor to the first floor for visitors   with disabilities.
"So, there is always a balancing exercise. We need to safeguard the architectural and historical integrity of the building while ensuring that it can continue to operate safely and inclusively in a contemporary environment."
RECREATING THE DETAILS
The restoration went beyond the stadium's structure.
Features that had disappeared over the years, including the original scoreboard and washrooms at the eastern terrace, were reconstructed.
Layers of paint were examined to determine the original colour scheme, while surviving pieces of mosaic tiles were used as references to reproduce tiles no longer commercially available.
Plastic seats installed in later years were also replaced with timber-strip seats based on the original design.
"These may seem like small details individually, but together they are what give Stadium Mer-deka its character and authenti-city," Izwan said.
KEEPING HERITAGE ALIVE
Restoring Stadium Merdeka, however, was only half the job.
The bigger challenge was ensuring it did not become a monument frozen in time.
Since reopening in August 2024, the stadium has hosted more than 200 events, including concerts, sporting events, arts and cultural programmes, educational activities, heritage tours, workshops and community events.
"Sometimes I am there during school sports days, and I love seeing the children running around the same grounds where Tunku Abdul Rahman said 'Merdeka' seven times 69 years ago.
"It is important to preserve that history while bringing the community along and allowing the next generation to experience it."
[[nid:1522493]]
That connection between heritage and the community, he said, was central to the restoration.
The benefits of heritage, however, extend beyond the stadium itself.
Izwan said historic buildings and neighbourhoods gave visitors a reason to experience Kuala Lumpur beyond its modern landmarks, allowing them to understand the country's history.
He said visitors to Stadium Merdeka can now see historical photographs of the first prime minister and the journey towards independence.
"We want people who visit the stadium to not only see a historic building but also understand the important role it played in our nation's history," he said.
Izwan said keeping heritage areas active throughout the year could also benefit businesses, food operators and attractions in surrounding neighbourhoods.
"Whatever advancement we make, it must ensure that our community benefits from it. That is why I never charge even one sen if people want to come to Stadium Merdeka to experience it.
He said the aim within the Merdeka 118 precinct is not only to draw visitors  to its attractions but also to encourage them to venture further into Kuala Lumpur's historic heart.
Through the wider Warisan KL agenda and initiatives such as Jelajah Warisan KL, visitors are encouraged to explore more of KL's historic heart,  including Stadium Negara, Petaling Street, Chinatown and Jalan Hang Tuah.
"For us, that is the bigger picture.
"We want the restoration of Stadium Merdeka and the development of the wider precinct to bring  people into the area, create more opportunities for the surrounding communities and encourage more people to discover this part of Kuala Lumpur's heritage."
[[nid:1522492]]
Warisan KL is a  heritage and culture-led urban rejuvenation initiative to revive the city's soul by restoring and reimagining its built heritage.
Its aim is to create a more liveable city while driving growth in tourism, community enterprise and commerce.
The 10  landmarks under the Warisan KL initiative include Bangunan Sultan Abdul Samad  and Dataran Merdeka, the Old Kuala Lumpur Railway Station, Masjid Negara, Dayabumi Complex, Carcosa and Seri Negara, Masjid Jamek, Stadium Merdeka and Merdeka 118 Precinct, Petaling Street, Medan Pasar, and Central Market.
Warisan KL unites government agencies, government-linked companies, government-linked investment companies, private partners and communities to position Kuala Lumpur as a vibrant hub of heritage, culture and creativity.

Title: Cloud seeding planned for areas with high API readings
Article:
Your browser does not support the audio element.
CLOUD seeding will be carried out in areas where the Air Pollutant Index (API) reading exceeds 150, especially those at 200 and above.
Deputy Prime Minister Datuk Seri Dr Ahmad Zahid Hamidi said the National Disaster Management Agency (Nadma), the Meteorological Department and the Royal Malaysian Air Force were already coordinating  such operations in haze-hit areas.
"Priority is given to areas where the API reading has reached 200," he said after launching Laman Usahawan Desa@Pameran Pertanian, Hortikultur dan Agropelancongan here yesterday.
Zahid, who is also Nadma chairman, said the operations were necessary due to declining water levels at several dams and reservoirs.
He added that cloud seeding would also depend on both need and suitability, as the presence of clouds alone did not guarantee they would reach the targeted areas.
"Even with clouds, we must consider their direction and whether they will move towards the intended locations."
Data from the Department of Environment's API Management System showed Sarawak had the country's worst readings.
An API reading of zero to 50 indicates good air quality, 51 to 100 is moderate, 101 to 200 is unhealthy, 201 to 300 is very unhealthy, and above 300 is hazardous.

Title: Before Nepal floods, China was asked for early warnings as risks mounted
Article:
KATHMANDU: Three months before a wall of water, mud and rock killed hundreds when it hurtled down a Himalayan valley bordering Nepal and China, experts and officials from both countries met in Kathmandu to discuss the risk of such disasters.
At the May 27 meeting in Nepal's capital, 10 officials from Nepal and about a dozen from China, including the Tibet region where the disaster struck, discussed strengthening cooperation to monitor and respond to floods, weather and glacier-related hazards, according to an agenda prepared by the Nepali side and seen by Reuters.
The participants called for joint risk-reduction measures, including inventories of glacial lakes and hazard mapping.
But two Nepali officials told Reuters they did not receive as much information as they wanted from China on glacier risks and water levels after the meeting and they feared insufficient data sharing could hamper their ability to anticipate and prepare for major disasters.
"What we actually wanted from them, and still want, is if there are early movements of glaciers and early movements around that area, we would want to know a bit early," said Sauhardra Joshi, a hydrologist at Nepal's Flood Forecasting Division, who was in the May meeting.
CHINA SAYS ITS DATA-SHARING HAS BEEN 'TIMELY'
No officials or experts have blamed either side for the natural disaster, which will cost an estimated tenth of Nepal's annual economic output to recover from. Nepali officials say the priority is to deepen cooperation with China.
China's foreign ministry did not respond to a request for comment on the May meeting or on Nepal's request for additional information sharing.
At the meeting, the Chinese said they did not have the mandate to sign an agreement to meet Nepal's requests, asking for further discussions, said Binod Parajuli, another Nepal government hydrologist.
Details of the meeting and Nepal's demands for broader cooperation in monitoring the glaciers that threaten communities on both sides of the border have not previously been reported.
China's embassy in Nepal said in a statement on X on Saturday that Beijing and Kathmandu had kept in close contact on the issue and had made "substantial progress" at the meeting in May on promoting cross-border disaster information sharing.
Nepal raised similar concerns last year, officials said, though experts and officials cautioned that what they describe as slow progress was not a significant factor in the latest disaster, in which a glacier collapse unleashed a catastrophic mudslide that has killed nearly 800 people in both countries and left more than 3,000 missing, by the latest count.
Rejecting criticism from some Nepali social media users that China had failed to provide adequate warning, the Chinese embassy said Chinese and international experts faced significant challenges monitoring hazards in the remote Himalayan region.
Chinese teams had shared important information with Nepal "in a timely manner", it said.
At last year's meeting, Nepal raised concerns about a flood in the same area, triggered by the sudden release of water from a glacial lake in Tibet that killed at least nine in Nepal and left more than a dozen missing.
"When the Chinese side sees a heavy precipitation forecast in the Tibet area, then they provide us that forecast and those observations," Parajuli said. But "not for avalanche and water level, landslides, extreme events."
China began sharing forecasts of heavy rain in Tibet over China's WeChat messaging app and email a month ago, Parajuli said.
TIMELINE TO CALAMITY
Twelve days before the disaster, China's World Meteorological Centre told Nepali officials in an email, seen by Reuters, that a monsoon depression was forecast for the area from Aug 14 to 19.
"Enhanced rainfall is likely across much of Nepal, and we wish to draw your attention to the potential for secondary and cascading hazards, including but not limited to landslides and flash floods," China warned.
The Chinese embassy said China has been sharing information including monitoring data on a lake formed by debris from last week's calamity.
The discussions over data-sharing underline the complexity of monitoring, forecasting and providing early warning in a region where regional geopolitical rivals — including China and India — control remote mountainous areas holding vast quantities of ice and snow that loom over densely populated South Asian plains.
Wednesday's catastrophe was sparked by the collapse of the glacier in a relatively unmonitored area, and a lack of bilateral cooperation was not a significant factor in Nepal's response, according to environmental anthropologist Austin Lord, senior fellow at the Washington-based Stimson Center think tank.
"That's not to forgive the fact that there isn't really a well-articulated system. And there is very limited exchange between Nepal and China," said Lord, who is part of a team supporting Nepal's government on disaster and climate risk management.
"Chinese scientists have a much greater capacity, have much greater resources for monitoring than those on the Nepal side overall."
The time that the torrent took to reach Nepal shows the value of early-warning systems, Parajuli said.
Around 8.32am Nepal time on Wednesday, the deluge blasted through a border crossing in Tibet as people attempted to flee, according to surveillance footage that has become a defining image of the disaster.
Twenty-six minutes later, Parajuli got a call from the chief of Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, alerting him to a flood on the Trishuli river. Parajuli's team found that a border monitoring station had not transmitted any data since 8.40.
"We also then tried to contact downstream stations, but downstream stations also couldn't post the data," leaving the team to suspect those devices had been washed away, he said.
After contacting local Nepali authorities to confirm the flooding, Parajuli said, his team sent a public alert to mobile phone users at 9.13.
At least four monitoring stations were destroyed by the flood that rampaged 168 km (104 miles) downstream from the Nepal-China border, carrying some 57.4 million cubic metres of water, more than half again as much as normal, according to a Nepali government assessment.
'HUGE GUSH OF MUD COMING STRAIGHT AT US'
Surging floodwaters, which dislodged giant boulders and pulled large buildings into the overflow, damaged 19 bridges and some 40km of highway, and knocked out more than 10pct of Nepal's power-generation capacity, according to the Stimson Center.
"It wasn't water. It was a huge gush of mud coming straight at us," said Keshav Prasad Baral of Tupche village, about 25km downstream of the border. "I tried to grab my wife's hand, but she was swept away by the mud."
When part of the glacier broke away, crashing to the valley floor hundreds of metres below, it unleashed high-speed flash floods, according to preliminary assessments by Nepali authorities.
The Hindu Kush Himalayas, home to hundreds of millions of people from Afghanistan to Myanmar, contain the world's largest volume of ice outside the poles, with more than 63,700 glaciers covering nearly 56,000 square km, almost the size of Croatia, and storing up to 5,700 cubic km of ice.
By comparison, the glacier chunk that caused the latest disaster carried an estimated 5 million cubic metres of ice and rock, according to Basanta Raj Adhikari, director of the Centre for Disaster Studies in Nepal's Tribhuvan University.
Driven by climate change, glacier melt is accelerating as snow cover declines and snowfall becomes more erratic, according to a 2023 study by the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development.
These changes will increase the likelihood of floods and landslides, as mountain communities also deal with such hazards as sedimentation and erosion, the centre projects.
Several of Nepal's major river systems originate in Tibet, then flow through one of the world's most seismically active and flood-prone regions.
Nepal's authorities will seek to work with China to conduct research and build systems to monitor avalanches and the release of water from glacial lakes — major risks for mountain communities — Parajuli said.
He said his department will propose a data-sharing agreement with China, along the lines of an arrangement that Nepal has with neighbouring India, for more frequent information on precipitation and river levels, not just high-precipitation forecasts.
Nepal will seek data every 10 minutes so that "we can warn our people, save our people," he said. "Our main target is we shouldn't miss any future disaster."--REUTERS

Title: Zambry: New committee to create framework for filling Auku vacuum
Article:
Your browser does not support the audio element.
AN independent committee will be established to study and recommend a framework for new legislation to replace the Universities and University Colleges Act 1971 (Auku).
Higher Education Minister Datuk Seri Dr Zambry Abd Kadir said yesterday repealing Auku required a transitional legal mechanism to avoid a legal vacuum, as it was the primary law governing public universities.
"If Auku is repealed without a replacement, how will our universities function? Without an overarching legal framework, universities cannot operate.
"Thus, a transitional legal mechanism must be put in place while we work on the new bill to ensure that institutional operations can run smoothly," he said at the launch of the Graduate Employability Strategic Plan 2026-2030 here.
Zambry said the reform process comprised four steps: forming the independent committee, conducting stakeholder engagement, establishing a drafting team to formulate the new bill, and putting in place the transitional mechanism.
He did not specify a deadline for the new legislation, saying the process would require thorough consultation.
Auku has 44 sections, with seven relating to students and the rest on matters including the establishment, administration and governance of universities.
Zambry added that the reform would also need to take into account other laws affecting higher education, including the Educational Institutions (Discipline) Act 1976, the Statutory Bodies (Discipline and Surcharge) Act 2000 and the Private Higher Educational Institutions Act 1996.
He said the repeal of Auku was in line with the ministry's long-term plan to introduce a single, comprehensive One Higher Education Act, outlined in the Malaysia Higher Education Blueprint 2026-2035.
He also acknowledged long-standing concerns about student and academic freedom under Auku and reiterated the government's commitment to a progressive and modern legal  framework.
"After 50 years of Auku, and given the dynamic evolution of our higher education landscape, we must review the framework  across all dimensions."
On Aug 16, Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim said Auku would be abolished and would not be replaced by another law that could curb student freedom.

Title: Grand Canyon flash flood: More than 20 feared missing [WATCH]
Article:
LOS ANGELES: More than 20 people may be missing after a flash flood in Grand Canyon National Park, the National Park Service said in a statement Sunday.
The floods hit the Bright Angel Canyon and Phantom Ranch area on Saturday, the service said, adding that it was working with Arizona authorities to evacuate people and account for individuals in the affected area.
The park service asked the public for any information about the missing, as well as any hikers who were in the area.
The flash flood began about 2.30pm on Saturday.
As of Sunday morning, 62 people have been evacuated, and others were scheduled to be evacuated, it said. No injuries have been reported so far.
The service warned that more thunderstorms and heavy rainfall were possible through Monday, possibly leading to "additional flash flooding, debris flows, rockfall and changing trail and river conditions." --AFP

Title: US strikes Iran for first time in a month
Article:
WASHINGTON: The United States said Sunday it had carried out strikes on Iranian rocket launchers on a small island in the Strait of Hormuz, its first attacks on Iran since late July.
"Earlier today, US forces struck two Iranian launchers on Larak Island," a US Central Command spokesman said, adding that Iran's Revolutionary Guards "were observed preparing to launch rockets with sea mines into the Strait of Hormuz."
The strikes came shortly after the US-Iran war hit the six-month mark, and at a time when hostilities had been subsiding.
In recent weeks, the Trump administration has prioritised "economic warfare" over military strikes against Iran.
Iran has effectively blocked the Strait of Hormuz, a strategic sea lane through which one-fifth of the world's oil passed before the United States and Israel started hostilities with airstrikes on Iran on Feb 28.
"Last week, CENTCOM completed clearing sea mines from the strait's international shipping routes," said Navy Captain Tim Hawkins, a spokesman for US Central Command.
"US forces are monitoring the area closely and remain prepared to protect the free flow of commerce through this essential waterway," he said.
Diplomatic efforts, spearheaded by mediators including Pakistan and Qatar, have tried for months to bring an end to the war to no avail.
While a ceasefire was agreed in April and a memorandum of understanding towards a final peace deal was signed in June, no agreement has been forthcoming and Washington has since declared "economic warfare" against Teheran.
A US naval counterblockade of Iranian ports is squeezing petrol supplies in Iran amid a shortfall of domestic production, as the US ramps up pressure on its foe.
The April ceasefire put an end to the most intense fighting, but sporadic attacks, mainly around the Strait of Hormuz, have dimmed the prospects of a final peace agreement.
In a statement on Friday, US Senator Jack Reed criticised President Donald Trump over the war.
"Six months later, not a single objective has been achieved," said Reed, the top Democrat on the Senate Armed Services Committee.
"Indeed, he has weakened our position in the Middle East and the world significantly."--AFP

Title: 'Venezuela owns its oil'
Article:
Your browser does not support the audio element.
INTERIM leader Delcy Rodriguez assured the public on Saturday that Venezuela retains control of its oil under a new agreement that allows the United States significant access to it.
The US will have majority control of 65 billion barrels of Venezuela's proven reserves in what President Donald Trump described on Friday as "the biggest oil deal in world history".
"One thing must be absolutely clear: Venezuela retains ownership and sovereignty over its resources," said Rodriguez in a speech on state television.
The agreement with the US aimed to turn "cold, inert" resources underground to "a source of social and economic well-being for the people of Venezuela", she said.
Caracas says the deal involves US$100 billion in private investment aimed at revitalising the industry in a country with the world's largest proven oil reserves.
But a lack of transparency is raising concerns among Venezuelans, including government supporters.
A flood of social media comments decried loss of sovereignty, meagre benefits and political costs.
"We don't know who this will benefit — whether it's Venezuela or (the US)," said Jesus Salazar, a security guard. "I have my doubts, but we'll have to wait and see what happens."
Venezuela's government has operated under intense pressure from the Trump administration since US forces ousted and captured long-time ruler Nicolas Maduro in January.
Washington has allowed Rodriguez, his vice-president, to stay on as interim leader so long as she toes Washington's line.
Venezuela's ruling party said on Saturday it supported economic measures that "prioritise national interests and make it possible to overcome the impact of more than a decade of economic sanctions, unilateral coercive measures, and unjust blockades".
The party consistently blames US sanctions for the collapse of Venezuela's economy.
Rodriguez has pushed through reforms in Venezuela's mining and petroleum industries, opening once tightly controlled sectors to private capital and foreign investment.
Washington, for its part, has eased sanctions imposed on the country's oil sector under the Maduro government.
Oil production rose by 29.8 per cent between January and July, reaching 1.2 million barrels per day (bpd) — still well below the three million bpd produced a quarter of a century ago.
The US deal aims to restore production to those levels, but analysts agree it would take time.
"The increase in production won't be seen for at least three or four years," said Oswaldo Felizzola, a professor at the Institute of Higher Studies in Administration, here.
He welcomed the US acting as a "guarantor" for investments in Venezuela, which has failed to attract significant capital for more than a decade. — AFP

Title: 69 years of Independence: Defining our vision for Malaysia
Article:
LETTER:
As we commemorate our 69th National Day on Aug 31, 2026, let us reflect on the meaning of Merdeka and the responsibilities that come with being a free and sovereign nation.
Over the past 69 years, Malaysia has made significant progress. We have built a diverse and vibrant nation, focussing on political stability and economic development.
But today, we face a very different and increasingly uncertain environment.
Economic pressures, geopolitical tensions, climate change, environmental challenges, technological disruption, serious corruption, social problems and concerns over safety and well-being are creating new challenges for our nation.
At home, issues such as road safety, crime, mental health, drug and substance abuse, ageing, environmental degradation and the erosion of social values require greater attention.
In facing these challenges, our greatest strength must continue to be unity.
Malaysia's diversity should never be viewed as a weakness. Our different races, religions, cultures and backgrounds are part of the Malaysian identity that we have built together.
We must reject hatred, extremism, intolerance and attempts to divide Malaysians.
The spirit of Merdeka must remind us that we are Malaysians first, and that our common future is more important than our differences.
The government has a fundamental responsibility to govern with integrity, competence, transparency and accountability.
It must ensure that public institutions are strong, that the rule of law is respected, that development benefits the people fairly, and that the safety, health and wellbeing of Malaysians remain not only a priority but a core value while the people also have their responsibilities.
We must respect the law, practice tolerance, protect our communities, care for the environment, reject corruption and irresponsible behaviour, and play our part in keeping our families, workplaces, schools and neighbourhoods safe.
A strong nation is not built by government policies alone. It is built every day by the conduct and values of its citizens.
We should also ask ourselves what kind of Malaysia we want to leave for the next generation.
We want a Malaysia where our children can grow up safely; where senior citizens can age with dignity; workers are protected; differences are respected; public spaces are safe; the environment is protected; and every Malaysian has an opportunity to live with dignity and hope.
As we look towards the future, we must move beyond merely celebrating our independence.
We must renew our faith and commitment to nation-building. Let us strengthen the spirit of the Rukun Negara and uphold its principles in our daily lives.
Let us place national interest above narrow interests and cooperation above confrontation.
The challenges ahead may be complex, but Malaysia has overcome difficult periods before. We can do so again if we remain united, responsible and committed to the common good.
On this 69th National Day, let us therefore make a renewed pledge:
That we will protect our unity.
That we will uphold our integrity.
That we will respect one another.
That we will safeguard our nation.
And that we will work together to build a safer, healthier, more harmonious and resilient Malaysia.
The future of Malaysia  belongs to all of us. May the spirit of Merdeka continue to inspire us to stand together, especially when times are difficult.
TAN SRI LEE LAM THYE
Unity Advocate
Kuala Lumpur

Title: Norway's new King Haakon VIII, popular face of shaken monarchy
Article:
AS comfortable in a duffel coat as in ceremonial dress, Norway's new monarch, King Haakon VIII, is the new face of a monarchy long praised for its modernity and modesty, but now beset by woe and scandal.
Haakon automatically succeeded to the throne Friday after his father, King Harald, passed away peacefully earlier in the day.
The 53-year-old informed the government in a meeting that he would keep the same motto as his father and grandfather: "All for Norway."
He has increasingly seen his family's affairs plastered across front pages: his wife's lung transplant, revelations about her ties to convicted US sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, a rape conviction against his stepson, and the escapades of his eccentric sister and her American self-proclaimed shaman husband.'
"Everything will be fine with him when the time comes. It is reassuring to know that," the late King Harald said of him in a book.
"I am fortunate that it is Crown Prince Haakon who has to take over," Harald said, musing that his own father had probably been more worried about the succession.
The tall, bearded and stately Haakon is as modest and measured as most Norwegians – reflecting a society that shuns opulence and ostentation.
Married to Mette-Marit, a commoner who was a single mother before their wedding, Haakon has focused his attention on issues that concern many of his generation, including environmental protection and fighting racism and homophobia.
"It's important that we protect who we are and for Norway to be a country where we're allowed to love and be with whoever we want," he said the day after a bloody attack against the gay community in Oslo in June 2022.
Born on July 20, 1973, the prince attended state-run daycare and schools, in line with the wishes of King Harald and Queen Sonja, who were keen to see him grow up among "ordinary" Norwegians.
After a stint in the navy, he went on to earn a bachelor's degree in political science at the University of California in Berkeley and a master's in international politics at the London School of Economics.
Haakon is a fan of skiing, surfing, and windsurfing, as well as music.
[[nid:1522353]]
It was at a 1999 music festival at Kristiansand, in southern Norway, that he met his future wife, whose tumultuous past made headlines in the Scandinavian country.
At the time, Mette-Marit Tjessem Hoiby was a single mother of a young son named Marius, the fruit of an earlier relationship with a man with a heavy criminal record, including assault and cocaine possession.
Norwegians however quickly saw beyond her wild past. The couple went on to have a daughter expected to one day be queen, Ingrid Alexandra, born in 2004, and a son Sverre Magnus, in 2005.
But storm clouds were building on the horizon.
Haakon's sister Princess Martha-Louise, a fan of alternative therapies, has repeatedly been accused of exploiting her royal title for commercial purposes.
She made headlines again by marrying a self-proclaimed shaman, Durek Verrett, in 2024, described as a dangerous "charlatan" by his critics.
Then his stepson Marius was arrested in August 2024 and sentenced to four years in prison in June 2026 for rape and assault. He has appealed.
Just days before the conviction, Haakon's wife Mette-Marit, underwent a lung transplant for pulmonary fibrosis that was diagnosed in 2018.
The Norwegian media had in February already published troubling revelations about Mette-Marit's friendship with Epstein in the early 2010s.
Even though the disgraced financier had already been convicted of soliciting a minor, Mette-Marit had been in frequent contact with him, their emails indicating a close relationship.
She said she had been "manipulated and deceived."
"When you get married, it's for better or for worse," Haakon remarked in March  during a televised interview the gave about the Epstein revelations.
The scandals have tarnished the royal family's image and weakened its support in the Scandinavian country, though it remains broadly popular.
Haakon has nevertheless "shown himself to be a man who remains steady in the face of a storm, and that is a very valuable quality in a monarch," Caroline Vagle, a reporter for magazine Se og Hor, told AFP.
"He has also had the best teacher he could possibly have had in his father," she added.
In a poll conducted in March, nearly eight out of 10 Norwegians felt that he would make a good king.
* The writer is from AFP

Title: Google Maps renames Lake Ontario 'Lake America' in US – but not Canada
Article:
WASHINGTON: Google redesignated Lake Ontario as "Lake America" on maps seen by US users Sunday after President Donald Trump announced he was renaming the body of water, with a Canadian official slamming the cross-border tensions as "absolutely backwards."
People in Canada will still see Lake Ontario, the Indigenous-rooted name used for the lake since the 17th century, on their devices and computers, the US-based tech giant said.
The shock nomenclatural spat erupted as the latest element of Trump's "America First" narrative, with longtime allies the United States and Canada ramping up a trade war that has seen Washington and Ottawa slap tit-for-tat tariffs on each other.
Apple's Maps app that comes installed on all iPhones makes no mention of "Lake America" on its maps as of Sunday morning.
Google said it made its change in line with the US Geographic Names Information System (GNIS), the official federal database for geographic names.
"Since we update Google Maps to reflect name changes in official government sources, which is GNIS for the US, people using Maps in the US will see 'Lake America,' those in Canada will continue to see 'Lake Ontario,' and those outside of the US and Canada will see both names," Google said on its blog.
The change mirrors Trump's unilateral altering of the name of the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America in January 2025 – a move Mexico has also rejected.
Ontario is the smallest by surface area of the five Great Lakes, which straddle the Canada-US border between Ontario province and the US state of New York.
The province's premier, Doug Ford, offered fresh criticism Sunday of the trade dispute and Trump's lake name change.
"It's absolutely backwards. It was like something out of (US comedy TV show) 'Saturday Night Live' when he signed a document saying – changed to 'Lake America.' No one's going to call it Lake of America," Ford told ABC talk show "This Week."
"It's just so disappointing."
Ford also warned that while a trade war would harm both countries, "it'd be definitely devastating on the US" given that Canada has been by far the largest purchaser of US vehicles. Should those buys dry up, US auto factories would be hit hard.
"A tariff on Canada is nothing more than a tax on American people," he said. "It's probably the worst move you could ever do."
Canada and the US have a deeply interconnected auto manufacturing sector, and a sizeable portion of parts for US vehicles are made in Canada.
Trump himself waded in Sunday to say Americans "want to make our own cars."
"Canada has been ripping us off for years – NO LONGER!" Trump posted on his Truth Social platform.
