Title: NASA launches Roman telescope on cosmic mapping mission
Article:
WASHINGTON: NASA launched its new flagship space telescope on Sunday, embarking on a multi-year mission to create an unprecedented map of the cosmos and shed light on some of the biggest mysteries in physics.
Designed to take a panoramic view of the vast reaches of space, the Roman Space Telescope "will help unlock the secrets of the universe," US President Donald Trump said Friday during a ceremony at NASA headquarters in Houston, Texas.
Standing over 12 metres (39 feet) tall, the state-of-the-art observatory launched from the Kennedy Space Centre in Florida at 7.26am (1126 GMT) aboard a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket.
Developed over more than a decade at a cost topping $4 billion, the telescope is named after pioneering US astronomer Nancy Grace Roman, who became known as the "Mother of Hubble," another of NASA's flagship telescopes.
While Hubble revealed that the universe is expanding faster than previously thought, Roman will seek to answer some of the other unsolved mysteries, including those of dark matter and dark energy.
"Roman will give the Earth a new atlas of the universe," NASA administrator Jared Isaacman said in April when he unveiled the project to the press.
STUDYING THE INVISIBLE
With a field of view more than 100 times larger than Hubble's – and significantly wider than James Webb's – Roman will survey vast swaths of the sky from a vantage point 1.5 million kilometers (930,000 miles) from Earth, which it will take about 100 days to reach.
Designed to work in tandem with other observatories such as Webb, which offers greater power and precision, Roman aims to discover thousands of exoplanets as well as tens of thousands of supernovae, the explosive deaths of massive stars.
"It will be the biggest catalog of astronomical objects anybody's ever produced, and it will help us understand how common are solar systems like our own," Dave Content, Roman's technical manager, told AFP.
The new telescope will also shed light on two of the biggest mysteries in physics: dark matter and dark energy. Their origins remain unknown, but together they are believed to make up about 95 percent of the universe.
Dark matter is thought to act as a kind of gravitational glue, while dark energy is believed to be a repulsive force driving the universe's expansion.
With its infrared vision, Roman will be able to detect light emitted by celestial objects billions of years ago, effectively looking back in time and offering scientists a glimpse into the universe's distant past and helping them better understand these two mysterious phenomena.
SURPRISE
Roman's observations will complement the work of the Rubin Observatory in Chile and the European Space Agency's (ESA) Euclid probe, and are highly anticipated because they could challenge scientists' understanding of the universe's structure.
Julie McEnery, Roman's senior project scientist, said recent research suggests the way scientists have been thinking about the universe's early expansion, based on the predictions of existing models, may be wrong.
"Recent observations hint that our standard model of the universe is incorrect," she told a press conference on Saturday, adding that Roman will help clear that up.
"It will definitively say, 'Yeah, the model works, or it doesn't.' And if it doesn't, it's going to provide us with the precision and quality of data that will allow us to start to distinguish between those options."
Scientists and the general public will have access to all of Roman's data. But the sheer volume will be daunting, Content warned.
The telescope will be generating about 1.3 terabytes of data a day, "which means you basically can't download the data to anybody's laptop," he said.
For McEnery, the more data, the better.
"I very much hope, and in fact expect, that the most exciting science from Roman will be a surprise, something we couldn't predict, and that will set the stage for the next deeper set of questions for future missions to address."

Title: Learn to belong to one another
Article:
DEAR Malaysia, I have been trying to remember when I first understood what it meant to belong to you. I don't think there was a moment.
I grew up in a household where nobody seemed interested in following the racial script. My Chinese grandparents insisted that I speak Bahasa Melayu, and speak it properly. My father, a Malay from Langkawi, insisted that I speak Hokkien and English. Apparently, everyone was worried someone else might neglect their cultural responsibilities.
So I grew up moving between languages without thinking much about which belonged to whom. They all belonged at home.
Only later did I realise that perhaps this was how I first knew you. Not through a flag or anthem, important as both would become, but around a family table where different languages, histories, food and opinions somehow occupied the same space.
Nobody called it multiculturalism. It was simply home.
And Malaysia, we have come a long way.
Every Merdeka, we return to 1957. We should. There is something profoundly moving about those old images: a young nation, a new flag and that magnificent word, Merdeka, called into the morning air.
But 69 years later, perhaps we owe that generation something more than remembrance.
They answered the great question of their time: Who should determine the future of this country?
Their answer was us.
Our question is harder: What kind of country will we make with that freedom?
A country can be independent long before all its people feel equally free. Free to aspire regardless of postcode or parentage. Free to disagree without having one's love for country questioned. Free, above all, to feel that Malaysia belongs as completely to you as to anyone else.
That is a more demanding Merdeka.
And I am enormously proud of what we have managed. We took a country divided by geography, ethnicity, religion and history and somehow made a home together. Imperfectly, noisily, occasionally exasperatingly, but together.
Living together requires compromise, curiosity and the humility to accept that no community has a monopoly on what it means to be Malaysian.
But Malaysia, love should not require blindness.
You have wounds.
There are children whose futures are shaped far too early by where they were born. Malaysians who work hard yet feel the ladder moving further away. Communities for whom national progress sometimes sounds more impressive in a speech than it feels in daily life.
We should be able to say this without being accused of loving you less.
Perhaps that is mature patriotism: not praise without question, but affection without illusion. To love a country is not to insist that it is flawless. It is to refuse to abandon it to its flaws.
And yet, I know another Malaysia.
I have spent most of my adult life in healthcare, and hospitals have taught me something about you.
Illness does not ask how you voted. Cancer has no interest in ethnicity. Fear sounds remarkably similar in every language. And when someone you love is frightened, the name on the badge of the nurse holding their hand matters much less than the fact that someone is holding it.
I have seen you there, Malaysia.
Different names, different prayers, different histories; people caring for people they might never otherwise have met.
The things we are told should separate us suddenly become smaller than the thing that joins us.
That Malaysia rarely makes the headlines. But I suspect it is closer to the truth of you than much of what does.
Dear Malaysia, we are not finished.
And neither is the work of independence.
Every generation has to defend its independence. What threatens that independence simply changes with time.
Today, sovereignty is less likely to be challenged by foreign soldiers marching through our streets. The pressures are quieter: economic dependence, technologies we use but do not own, data we generate but do not control, knowledge we consume but do not create.
This does not mean turning away from the world.
We must remain open to trade, investment, ideas and technology. But openness and dependence are not the same thing.
Perhaps that is our generation's Merdeka: to engage the world confidently without surrendering our ability to choose our own future.
Countries are not heirlooms. They do not remain independent simply because a previous generation won independence for them.
Each generation gets Malaysia on loan.
For a little while, it is our turn to decide what we will build, what we will protect, what we will refuse to lose and what we will hand to those who come after us.
So, Malaysia, what do I wish for you?
Not perfection.
I wish you the confidence to make room for all your children. The courage to see honestly where you have fallen short. And the wisdom never to mistake our differences for weakness.
The flag is easy to raise. The harder work is building a country in which every Malaysian can look at it and know, without qualification, that it is theirs.
Because perhaps the deepest promise of Merdeka was never simply that you would belong to us.
It was that we would learn to belong to one another.
Selamat Hari Merdeka, Malaysia.
With love,
One of your own
P.S. Malaysia, don't change too much. Just the things we both know you should.
The writer is chief executive officer of IHH Healthcare Malaysia
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: A childhood between nations
Article:
FOREIGN policy is usually written as the history of governments. We remember communiqués, treaties, summits and the men and women who negotiated them.
Much less is written about the families who travelled with diplomats: spouses who rebuilt  homes in unfamiliar cities, and children who moved between countries without quite understanding that the world unfolding around them would one day become history.
I was one of those children.
I was born in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, into a Malaysian diplomatic household when Malaysia itself was still finding its place in the post-colonial world.
As an infant, I was bathed in Zamzam water and carried in tawaf around the Kaaba. Jeddah was more than the place of my birth. It was becoming an important centre of Malaysia's engagement with the Muslim world.
Tunku Abdul Rahman had left the premiership but remained active in  public life. He became the first secretary-general of the Organisation of the Islamic Conference (OIC), and was involved in the preparatory work preceding the establishment of the Islamic Development Bank.
Malaysia, though geographically on the eastern edge of the Muslim world, was actively participating  in its emerging multilateral institutions.
My own memories are rather less statesmanlike. I was apparently an energetic boy. At home, however, I had an extraordinary tendency to fall asleep when my parents entertained.
Tunku noticed. He would sometimes tease my late father in his characteristic Kedah dialect: "Osman,
hang bagi ubat tidoq kat dia ka
?" (Osman, did you give him sleeping medicine?)
It is a small memory. But history is sometimes best remembered through small things.
WHEN DIPLOMACY WAS ALSO A FAMILY AFFAIR
Our family's diplomatic journey later took us to Jakarta, where my father was seconded to the Asean Secretariat.
If Jeddah represented Malaysia's engagement with the wider Muslim world, Jakarta represented something geographically closer but politically no less ambitious: the construction of a Southeast Asian regional order among countries emerging from colonialism and conflict.
My father served during the tenures of two successive Asean secretaries-general, Chan Kai Yau of Singapore and Phan Wannamethee of Thailand, and enjoyed good working relationships with both.
Asean itself was still young. Founded in 1967, with its secretariat established in 1976, the institution we now take for granted — with its summits, economic agreements and extensive networks of regional cooperation — was still being built.
And institutions are not built only by leaders. They depend equally on people who administer budgets, organise meetings, prepare papers, manage personnel and make organisations function from one day to the next.
Diplomacy has its glamorous moments, but much of international cooperation is constructed quietly through competence, persistence and trust.
Jakarta gave me another education altogether.
Our neighbour was Dr Raden Soeharto Sastrosoeyoso, an Indonesian physician whose life intersected with the founding generation of the republic.
He had served as personal physician to president Sukarno and was associated with institution-building in independent Indonesia. Decades later, Indonesia would formally recognise him as a national hero.
I would sometimes visit his residence and listen as he spoke about Indonesia. I remember hearing about Budi Utomo and Sarekat Dagang Islam, the role of doctors in Indonesia's nationalist awakening, and figures such as Dr Cipto Mangunkusumo.
I was too young to appreciate the privilege. Only much later did I understand that I had been listening not merely to stories about history, but to someone whose own life had passed through it.
There was a historical symmetry to those Jakarta years that escaped me then.
Next door was a man connected to the generation that helped create the Indonesian nation. At my father's workplace was an institution devoted to ensuring that Southeast Asia's nations could coexist and cooperate.
One represented the great political project of the first half of the 20th century: national independence. The other represented one of the great projects of its second half: regional cooperation. The first generation had to establish sovereignty. The generation that followed discovered that sovereignty alone was insufficient.
Independent countries still needed trade, stability, dialogue and institutions capable of managing differences without allowing them to become conflicts.
THE QUIET EDUCATION OF A DIPLOMAT'S CHILD
That is where Jeddah and Jakarta ultimately converge.
For Malaysia's early diplomats, diplomacy was seldom theirs alone. A foreign posting uprooted an entire household. Spouses adapted to unfamiliar societies and responsibilities; children changed schools, friends, languages and countries.
Home might temporarily be Jeddah, Jakarta or another foreign city before Malaysia became home again — until the next posting.
The children understood little of the diplomacy, but they received another kind of education. They discovered that countries looked different when viewed from beyond their borders, and that foreigners were not abstractions but classmates, neighbours and friends. They also learnt that being Malaysian did not require being insulated from the world.
Exposure to other societies could sharpen rather than diminish one's understanding of home.
My childhood began in Jeddah,  a city anchored  in Islam's most sacred geography, as Malaysia expanded its engagement with the Muslim world. It continued in Jakarta while Asean was developing its institutional foundations and an elderly Indonesian doctor introduced me to the nationalism that had preceded regionalism.
None of this followed a plan.
A child does not know that he is witnessing foreign policy. He remembers photographs, visitors and dinner conversations; unfamiliar cities and new schools; his father's office; an elderly neighbour telling stories; and a former prime minister joking because the boy has fallen asleep again.
Only decades later do the pieces acquire meaning.
Perhaps this is why diplomacy should not be understood solely through official archives.
Archives tell us what governments decided. The memories of diplomatic families tell us something different: what it felt like when a young nation first encountered the world.
Malaysia's first post-Merdeka diplomatic generations helped establish relationships and institutions that subsequent generations inherited. Their families travelled quietly beside them, carrying fragments of those encounters home. I happened to be one of those children.
And somewhere between Jeddah and Jakarta, between Tunku Abdul Rahman and an old Indonesian doctor, between the OIC and Asean, I began to understand a lesson that has stayed with me ever since:
Malaysia may be our home, but Malaysia has never existed apart from the world.
The writer is an adjunct lecturer at Universiti Teknologi Petronas and senior consultant with Global Asia Consulting
The opinion expressed are his own

Title: NST Leader: The chicken-and-egg crisis nobody's solving
Article:
RISING chicken and egg prices, driven  by  closures of problematic poultry farms, are an upshot of the old chicken-and-egg paradox.
On one hand, chicken and egg production is going great guns. On the other hand, it's plagued by fly infestations, labour shortages, rising feed costs and regulatory pressure.
Despite the incongruity, farms do meet domestic demand, but national supply is tight.
Because of these problems, seven farms, mainly in Negri Sembilan, recently closed, affecting the production of 3.7 million live chickens.
According to the Federation of Livestock Farmers' Associations of Malaysia, the affected farms were suspended and fined, though some reopened after improving operations.
Still, the industry thinks 40 to 50 per cent of small and medium-sized farms nationwide have closed or stopped production due to structural and financial crises. If chicken and egg prices have suddenly jumped beyond RM9 to RM9.50 per kg and RM13.89 to RM14.79 per tray, respectively, you'll know why.
Farms face a cause-and-effect dilemma: higher feed costs, especially from volatile  global imports, and labour shortages raise production costs and stifle operations.
Because the market cap on poultry prices was removed, supply and prices remain volatile. If supply shrinks, the result is  over-reliance on costlier imports. While dependence on foreign labour is still being negotiated, it creates policy contradictions.
The government urges  fewer foreign workers, but farms insist they cannot harvest without the migrants.
Mechanisation is the answer, but farmers baulk at high capital investments, complex farm structures and long maturity periods.
To set aside the chicken-and-egg paradox, the government should start with a better labour supply —  unrealistic quotas can't handle manure management and cleaning.
Farm operators and workers are ageing: 460,000 are 60 and above, while 327,000 are aged 46-59. To improve  farm costs and profitability, consolidate the land and farms.
Allow farmers to own and combine separate parcels under a single management — creating economies of scale without transferring ownership — through rental, management fee and profit-sharing models.
After all, this principle was set out  under the National Agrofood Policy 2021–2030 2.0 to resolve chronic food import issues and improve livelihoods.
To cut imported feed and fertiliser, government agricultural companies can expand  domestic production instead of relying on imported raw ingredients.
Enforcement should distinguish between deliberate violations and real struggles to meet standards.
Farmers lamented that a viable farm takes years and good money: estimates go as high as RM60 million to raise birds in a closed-house system, excluding land costs.
Rather than subsidise consumers, subsidise farmers. Despite a plausible route to viability, the chicken-and-egg contradiction  will still persist in policy: will pushing for higher compliance and cleaner operations end up closing farms, reducing supply and pushing prices higher?
While regulation is necessary, enforcement must be practical enough not to drive legitimate farmers out of business and threaten  food security.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Police hunt driver after man killed while crossing Shah Alam road
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR, Aug 31 — Police are hunting for the driver of an unidentified vehicle believed to have struck a 45-year-old pedestrian, killing him in Shah Alam this morning.
Harian Metro
reported that the crash happened at about 8.20am along Jalan Bukit Kemuning, in the direction from Taman Sri Muda towards Klang.
Shah Alam district police chief Assistant Commissioner Sarudin Samah said the victim, who is from Bangladesh, was believed to have been crossing the road when he was hit.
“As a result of the collision, the victim suffered severe injuries to his head and legs and was pronounced dead at the scene.
“The victim’s body was later taken to the Forensic Department at Shah Alam Hospital for a post-mortem examination,” he said today.
Sarudin said the vehicle involved has yet to be identified, with police carrying out further investigations to trace both the vehicle and its driver.
The case is being investigated under Section 41(1) of the Road Transport Act 1987.
Police have also appealed for anyone with information about the crash to come forward.
“Members of the public with information about the incident are urged to come forward to assist investigations by contacting investigating officer Inspector Abdul Nasser Peping of the Traffic Investigation and Enforcement Division at the Shah Alam district police headquarters at 012-286 3875,” Sarudin said.

Title: Four suspects remanded after 29‑year‑old slashed with sharp weapons in brutal Kajang roadside attack
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR, Aug 31 — Police have detained four men to assist investigations into a man who was found seriously injured after being attacked with sharp weapons by the roadside near Taman West Country, Kajang early Saturday morning.
Kajang district police chief ACP Naazron Abdul Yusof said a police report regarding the 29-year-old victim was lodged at 2.28am and the victim is currently receiving treatment at Kajang Hospital.
“The victim is being treated for serious injuries believed to have been caused by an attack with sharp weapons by several individuals known to him.
“The Kajang District Police Headquarters Criminal Investigation Division launched an operation to track down the suspects and successfully detained four local male suspects aged between their 20s and 30s around Kajang yesterday and early this morning,” he said in a statement here yesterday.
He said all the suspects had several criminal and drug-related records and had been remanded for four days until Wednesday (Sept 2) to assist investigations.
He said the case was being investigated under Section 307 of the Penal Code for attempted murder and Section 148 of the Penal Code for rioting while carrying weapons or something that could be used as a weapon.
“Initial urine screening found that one of the suspects tested positive for methamphetamine, and the suspect is also being investigated under Section 15(1)(a) of the Dangerous Drugs Act 1952 for allegedly self-administering drugs,” he said.
He said further investigations were underway to establish the motive for the incident and trace other individuals linked to the case, as well as gather information related to the incident.
He said anyone with information on the incident is urged to come forward to assist investigations by contacting Investigating Officer Insp Sharulhasram Ramli at 017-2530 380 or any nearby police station. — Bernama

Title: Snatch thieves fail to grab woman’s handbag, but rip RM2,000 gold bracelet from her wrist outside Cheras home
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR, Aug 31 — Two men on a motorcycle targeted a 49-year-old woman outside her home in Cheras, failing to snatch her handbag before ripping a RM2,000 gold bracelet from her wrist and speeding away.
Harian Metro
reported that the woman was answering a phone call in front of her house when the pair approached on a Yamaha Y15ZR motorcycle at about 11.15am yesterday.
Kajang district police chief Assistant Commissioner Naazron Abdul Yusof said one of the men got off the motorcycle and initially tried to seize the victim’s handbag.
“A Yamaha Y15ZR motorcycle carrying two unidentified male suspects approached the victim, and one of the suspects got off and tried to pull away her handbag but failed.
“The suspect then snatched a gold bracelet worn on the victim’s left wrist before fleeing with his accomplice,” he said today.
Naazron said the woman was not injured in the incident, although she lost the bracelet, which was valued at RM2,000.
Police received a report at 3.44pm yesterday over the snatch theft.
Police reviewing closed-circuit television footage from the area found that the suspects were wearing helmets with dark visors, while the motorcycle’s registration number could not be clearly made out.
Naazron said police were working to identify and track down the suspects to assist investigations under Section 395 of the Penal Code.
The case had earlier drawn attention on social media after photographs and video clips showing individuals believed to be the suspects were uploaded on Threads.
Anyone with information may contact the nearest police station or investigating officer Inspector Muhammad Aidhil Othman at 019-371 3937.

Title: Family outing turns to tragedy as father and eight-year-old son drown off Pengerang
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR, Aug 31 — A family outing ended in tragedy when a 33-year-old father and his eight-year-old son drowned off the coast near a campsite in Pengerang, Johor, last night.
Utusan Malaysia
reported that the victims were identified as Mohammad Nizam Zainal and his son, Muhammad Zamri Mikhail.
The pair were found unconscious after members of the public pulled them ashore near the campsite in Kampung Punggai before firefighters arrived.
Punggai Fire and Rescue Station operations commander Aldron Dey Judih@Judeh said an emergency call was received at 7.10pm.
Six firefighters were sent to the scene with a Fire Rescue Tender and a four-wheel-drive vehicle.
“Upon the arrival of the operations team at the scene, the two victims were found unconscious after members of the public had brought them ashore before the firefighters arrived.
“The operations team performed cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) on both victims,” he said in a statement, according to
Utusan Malaysia
.
The boy was then taken to the Bayu Damai Health Clinic in a family car, while his father was transported there in a Punggai fire station Hilux for further treatment.
“However, both victims were pronounced dead by the medical officer on duty upon arrival at the clinic,” Aldron said.
The fire and rescue operation ended at 8.10pm.

Title: Serian API nears 500 as four Sarawak areas hit hazardous levels
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR, Aug 31 — Air pollution in Serian reached a hazardous Air Pollutant Index (API) reading of 476 this morning, as four areas in Sarawak recorded readings above the 300 mark.
Data from the Department of Environment’s Air Pollutant Index Management System (APIMS) showed Serian recording the highest reading at 8.20am, followed by Samarahan at 330, Sri Aman at 326 and Kuching at 317.
All four readings fall within the hazardous category.
Under Malaysia’s API classification, readings above 300 are considered hazardous, while those between 201 and 300 are classified as very unhealthy.
Several other parts of Sarawak were also experiencing very unhealthy air quality, with Sarikei recording an API of 267, Sibu 219 and Mukah 214.
APIMS data also showed another 14 locations across six states and territories recording unhealthy API levels above 100.
In Sarawak, they included Samalaju, Miri, ILP Miri, Kapit, Bintulu and Limbang.
Unhealthy readings were also recorded in Sungai Petani in Kedah; Labuan; Seberang Jaya, Seberang Perai and Minden in Penang; Tawau and Politeknik Kota Kinabalu in Sabah; and Taiping in Perak.

Title: King Sultan Ibrahim and Queen Raja Zarith Sofiah grace Putrajaya’s grand 69th National Day parade
Article:
PUTRAJAYA, Aug 31 — Malaysia’s King and Queen, Their Majesties Sultan Ibrahim and Raja Zarith Sofiah, graced the 69th National Day celebration at Dataran Putrajaya today.
This marks the third year Their Majesties have witnessed the grand spectacle, following Sultan Ibrahim’s oath-taking and installation as the 17th Yang di-Pertuan Agong on Jan 31 and July 20, 2024, respectively.
Their Majesties arrived at 8am and were received by Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim and his wife, Datuk Seri Dr. Wan Azizah Wan Ismail, as well as Communications Minister Datuk Seri Fahmi Fadzil, who also serves as chairman of the National Day and Malaysia Day (HKHM) 2026 Main Committee.
The resonant call of the trumpet echoed across Dataran Putrajaya before the Main Honour Guard band played the national anthem,
Negaraku
.
This was followed by a fly-past of five helicopters carrying the Malaysian flag and the flags of the Malaysian Armed Forces, Army, Royal Malaysian Navy and Royal Malaysian Air Force, immediately after Their Majesties took their places at the Royal Stage.
Sultan Ibrahim also inspected the parade and received the Royal Salute from the Main Honour Guard, performed by the 41st Battery of the Ceremonial Royal Artillery Regiment, comprising three officers and 57 other personnel from Sungai Buloh Camp.
Themed “Malaysia Madani: Kesejahteraan Dinikmati”, this year’s parade is expected to draw over 80,000 visitors and features 10,819 parade members across 76 contingents and 22 brass bands. — Bernama

Title: Ong Kian Ming quits DAP after 14 years, rules out GE16 run but vows to campaign for Khairy
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR, Aug 31 — Former Bangi MP Ong Kian Ming has resigned from DAP after 14 years, ruling out contesting the next general election or joining another political party in the near future while reaffirming his pledge to campaign for Khairy Jamaluddin if he stands in the next general election (GE16).
Ong announced his departure in a Facebook post today addressed to DAP secretary-general Anthony Loke and copied to the party’s national organising secretary Khoo Poay Tiong.
“I am writing to inform you that I am resigning as a member of the Democratic Action Party (DAP) effective on the 31st of August 2026,” he wrote.
Ong, who joined DAP in 2012, did not give a reason for his resignation and struck an appreciative tone as he reflected on his years with the party.
During that period, he served as MP for Serdang from 2013 to 2018 and Bangi from 2018 to 2022, as well as deputy international trade and industry minister between 2018 and 2020.
He was also an appointed member of DAP’s central executive committee from 2019 to 2022 and an elected member of the party’s Selangor state committee from 2018 to 2024.
“I am grateful to have been given the opportunity to contribute to the party and the country in different ways since I joined the party in 2012,” Ong said.
He singled out former DAP leaders Tony Pua and Lim Guan Eng for thanks, crediting Pua with inviting him to join the party and providing guidance over the past 14 years.
Ong also expressed gratitude to Lim for giving him the opportunity to contest the parliamentary seats of Serdang and Bangi and to serve as a deputy minister during Lim’s tenure as DAP secretary-general.
He also thanked DAP members and leaders in Serdang and Bangi whom he worked with during his nine years as an MP.
The former lawmaker made clear, however, that his resignation would not be followed by an immediate switch to another party or another attempt to enter Parliament.
“I am not planning to join another political party in the near future and I will not be seeking to contest as a candidate in the next general election (GE16),” he said.
But Ong said his departure from DAP had not changed a promise he made earlier this year to support Khairy, with whom he has maintained a friendship despite their years on opposing sides of Malaysian politics.
“I remain committed to fulfil the promise I made on the 10th of January 2026, to help Khairy Jamaluddin campaign in GE16, if he is given a seat to run in,” he said.
In January, Ong said he was prepared to take leave from work to campaign publicly for Khairy in GE16 regardless of which political party the former health minister represented.
Ong said today that he intended to continue contributing to the country outside elected politics, including through his “Are We OK” podcast, his advisory roles and by working with others who share similar interests.
His resignation comes two weeks after DAP delegates voted overwhelmingly for the party’s ministers and deputy ministers to remain in the federal government until the end of the current parliamentary term.
Ong had weighed in extensively ahead of the August 16 vote, outlining arguments both for remaining in government and for leaving Cabinet as a means of putting greater pressure on Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim to deliver promised reforms.
He ended his resignation announcement with a brief Merdeka Day message: “Happy Merdeka Day!”

Title: Tens of thousands gather before sunrise as favourable weather lifts National Day spirit
Article:
PUTRAJAYA, Aug 31 — Dataran Putrajaya came alive this morning as tens of thousands of visitors gathered for the 2026 National Day celebrations.
A Bernama check found that as early as 3.30am, visitors of all ages were already braving the pre-dawn darkness and walking several kilometres from their parking spots to secure places near the main stage.
The spirit of independence was clearly reflected in the turnout, with parents bringing their young children in pushchairs and people with disabilities in wheelchairs also joining the celebrations.
To ensure public safety and smooth traffic flow amid the large crowds, police have been closely monitoring traffic along the main routes around Dataran Putrajaya since early this morning.
The favourable weather this morning added to the festive and patriotic mood as Malaysians gathered to celebrate National Day.
According to the Department of Environment (DOE)’s Malaysian Air Pollutant Index Management System (APIMS) portal, the Air Pollutant Index (API) reading at the Putrajaya station stood at 79, indicating a moderate level.
Themed “Malaysia Madani: Kesejahteraan Dinikmati”, the celebration is expected to draw about 80,000 visitors and will feature a line-up of performances to enhance the patriotic spirit among those at Dataran Putrajaya and viewers watching the event live on television. — Bernama

Title: PM Anwar joins Cabinet and thousands at Dataran Putrajaya for Malaysia’s 69th National Day parade
Article:
PUTRAJAYA, Aug 31 — Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim and members of the Cabinet today joined thousands of Malaysians in celebrating the 69th National Day at Dataran Putrajaya, here.
Anwar, who is also Finance Minister, and his wife Datuk Seri Dr Wan Azizah Wan Ismail arrived at the royal stage at 7.53am as the Hormat Perdana song was played.
Earlier, Deputy Prime Minister Datuk Seri Dr Ahmad Zahid Hamidi arrived at Dataran Putrajaya at 7.45am.
Also present were Communications Minister Datuk Seri Fahmi Fadzil, who is also chairman of the main committee for the 2026 National Day and Malaysia Day (HKHM) celebrations, Home Minister Datuk Seri Saifuddin Nasution Ismail, Defence Minister Datuk Seri Mohamed Khaled Nordin and other Cabinet ministers.
Deputy ministers, dignitaries and foreign delegates were also among those attending the 69th National Day celebrations, themed “Malaysia Madani: Kesejahteraan Dinikmati”.
The event will feature 10,819 participants from 76 contingents and 22 marching bands, alongside 11 decorated cars, 328 land, sea and air assets, 112 working animals and 22 electric vehicle (EV) assets. — Bernama

Title: Building Merdeka: How the nation‑building projects of 1957-65 shaped the early years of independence
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR, Aug 31 — Before Malaya had even become independent, it was already building the place where independence would be declared.
The foundation stone for Stadium Merdeka was laid in February 1957, months before the country was due to end British rule.
Construction was accelerated and the stadium was completed in just six months, opening on August 30 — one day before Merdeka.
The following morning, it became the stage for one of the defining moments in the country’s history.
At Stadium Merdeka, Malaysia’s first Prime Minister Tunku Abdul Rahman proclaimed the independence of the Federation of Malaya.
A man walks past giant poster of Tunku Abdul Rahman during the declaration of Independence at the ‘Jalan Merdeka Exhibition’, an exhibition celebrating the history of our Independence Day at Carcosa and Seri Negara August 13, 2018. — Picture by Azneal Ishak
It was an appropriate beginning for a country about to embark on a very different kind of construction project.
Over the next eight years, Kuala Lumpur acquired a national stadium, international-class hotels, Parliament House, a national museum, a national mosque, a national language institution, a major water-supply dam and a new international airport.
Some were grand symbols. Others were decidedly practical.
Together, however, they reveal what a young country thought independence should look like.
It was not enough to have sovereignty on paper.
Our fledgling country needed institutions to govern itself, infrastructure to support its growing population and economy, and national symbols through which its people could begin to see themselves as part of something larger than the territories and communities they had inherited.
The result was a burst of construction that turned independence into something that could be seen, entered, used and experienced.
Stadium Merdeka was designed by British architect Stanley Edward Jewkes. — Picture by Firdaus Latif
A country announcing itself
Stadium Merdeka was perhaps the clearest expression of the new nation’s confidence.
Built specifically to accommodate the independence celebrations, its completion in time for Merdeka was itself a statement of intent.
The stadium was designed by British architect Stanley Edward Jewkes, who was also involved in several major post-war public works in Malaya.
Its sweeping cantilevered roof and open seating bowl created a modern structure capable of holding tens of thousands of people.
More importantly, its first great event was not a sporting match.
It was independence.
The choice of a new stadium rather than an existing colonial-era venue gave the declaration a purpose-built setting — a national space created for a sovereign country at the precise moment it came into being.
Federal Hotel opened three days before Merdeka to accommodate foreign dignitaries and overseas guests attending the independence celebrations. — Picture courtesy of The Federal Kuala Lumpur
The Federal Hotel, which opened in Bukit Bintang on August 28, 1957, offered another glimpse of what the new capital wanted to become.
Its opening came just three days before independence, and its original 90 rooms were used to accommodate foreign dignitaries and overseas guests arriving for the celebrations.
It was described as the first international-class hotel in the country.
That was more than a matter of comfort.
A newly independent capital needed to receive diplomats, businessmen, tourists and other international visitors.
Kuala Lumpur was beginning to present itself not simply as the administrative centre inherited from the British, but as the capital of a modern country with ambitions beyond its colonial past.
The pattern continued.
Stadium Negara opened in 1962 as the country’s first indoor stadium, giving Kuala Lumpur another major venue for sports, exhibitions and public events.
The capital was acquiring the physical infrastructure of a city that expected to host the world.
A general view of the Parliament building in Kuala Lumpur November 6, 2025. The new Parliament complex was completed in time for Malaysia’s formation. — Picture by Yusof Isa
A country building its own institutions
The most important projects, however, were not necessarily the most spectacular.
They were the buildings that gave the new state somewhere to govern, preserve its history and define its identity.
Parliament was perhaps the most literal example.
The Federation of Malaya’s first Parliament had met in a converted building on Jalan Ampang in 1959.
A permanent complex was subsequently planned on a 16.2-hectare site near the Lake Gardens.
Construction began in 1962 after the foundation stone was laid by Tunku Abdul Rahman on August 31 that year.
The site had to be transformed before the building could rise. A hill was levelled and the complex — comprising a three-storey main block and 17-storey tower — was completed in roughly a year at a cost of RM18 million.
The building’s distinctive roof structures and tower made it one of Kuala Lumpur’s most recognisable landmarks.
Its symbolism was even more significant.
Malaysia’s first Parliament sat for the first time in the new complex on September 16, 1963 — the day the new federation itself was formed.
The building therefore became part of the physical birth of Malaysia.
Even the foundation stone contained objects representing the country: a copy of the first House of Representatives Hansard, newspapers, Malaysian currency, tin ore, rubber and paddy.
The message was simple enough.
The new state was being built from its own institutions, resources and political system.
General view of the mosaic mural at Dewan Bahasa dan Pustaka in Kuala Lumpur December 30, 2025. — Picture by Firdaus Latif.
Defining the nation
Other buildings addressed a less straightforward question: what exactly was this new country?
Dewan Bahasa dan Pustaka provided one answer.
The institution had moved to Kuala Lumpur in 1957 and was given statutory status in 1959.
It subsequently moved into its own building on Jalan Lapangan Terbang Lama in 1962.
Its task was to develop and promote the Malay language and literature, making it an important institution in the effort to establish Bahasa Melayu within the life of the new country.
The building therefore represented an aspect of independence that was less visible than a stadium or Parliament.
Political independence had changed who governed the country.
National institutions would help determine how that country spoke about itself.
A general view at the Muzium Negara in Kuala Lumpur June 11, 2025. Construction began in 1959 and the museum opened on August 31, 1963, shortly before the formation of Malaysia. — Picture by Yusof Mat Isa
Muzium Negara offered another way of doing the same thing.
Construction began in 1959 and the museum opened on August 31, 1963 — shortly before the formation of Malaysia.
Its architecture drew heavily on local traditions, incorporating Malay vernacular influences alongside elements associated with traditional Malay and Minangkabau architecture.
The building itself thus became part of the story it was designed to tell.
A national museum was not merely a place to keep artefacts.
It was a place to assemble a national past.
By 1963, the question of that past had become more complicated.
Malaya was becoming Malaysia, bringing Sabah, Sarawak and Singapore into a new federation.
The country now needed to accommodate different histories and identities within a common national framework.
The museum, like the language institution, became part of that wider effort to give the new federation a sense of continuity and identity.
Visitors take pictures in front of Masjid Negara on the first day of Hari Raya Aidilfitri April 10, 2024. Tunku Abdul Rahman rejected a proposal for it to bear his name and instead chose Masjid Negara — the National Mosque. — Picture by Choo Choy May.
Modernity, with a Malaysian face
Masjid Negara took another approach to the same challenge.
The idea of a national mosque had emerged around the time of independence.
Tunku Abdul Rahman rejected a proposal for it to bear his name and instead chose Masjid Negara — the National Mosque.
Construction was completed in 1965.
Its architecture was strikingly modern.
The most recognisable feature is its large folded roof, designed in the form of an open umbrella.
The design reflected Malaysia’s tropical environment while incorporating local and Malay architectural influences.
A general view of Masjid Negara in Kuala Lumpur on August 22, 2026. The most recognisable feature of Masjid Negara is its large folded roof, designed in the form of an open umbrella. — Picture by Firdaus Latif
Its 73-metre minaret gave the building a powerful presence in the Kuala Lumpur skyline.
The mosque therefore combined several ideas that the young country was trying to reconcile: Islam, Malay architectural traditions, a tropical environment and modern construction.
It was not a replica of an older architectural model.
It was a national building created in the language of a country that wanted to be modern while retaining a recognisably local identity.
That balance would recur across the architecture of the period.
The buildings were modern, but they did not necessarily look like they could have been built anywhere.
Building what the city needed
For all the symbolism of the national landmarks, independence also required less glamorous infrastructure.
The Klang Gates Dam was completed in 1958 as the first dam in Malaysia built for water supply.
Its purpose was straightforward: provide water for a growing Kuala Lumpur and the surrounding area.
A general view of the entrance to the Klang Gate Dam in Kuala Lumpur on August 29, 2026. — Picture by Firdaus Latif.
Yet projects like this were just as important to the country’s development ambitions as the buildings carrying national names.
A capital could not expand without reliable water.
Nor could a growing economy function without transport infrastructure.
That was the thinking behind Subang Airport.
A view of the Sultan Abdul Aziz Shah Airport SkyPark Terminal in Subang July 23, 2024. Opened on August 30, 1965, with what was then South-east Asia’s longest runway, connecting the young country to the wider region and world. — Picture by Raymond Manuel
Construction began in 1961 and the airport opened on August 30, 1965, replacing Sungai Besi as Kuala Lumpur’s main airport.
Its 3.7-kilometre runway was then the longest in South-east Asia.
Subang was built for a country that expected its connections with the outside world to grow.
It would allow Malaysia to handle larger aircraft and increasing international traffic while strengthening Kuala Lumpur’s position as a regional centre.
The contrast with Stadium Merdeka was striking.
One building marked the moment the country became independent.
The other was designed for the country that independence was expected to produce.
Stadium Merdeka was built specifically to accommodate the independence celebrations, its completion in time for Merdeka was itself a statement of intent. — Pictures courtesy of PNB
The timing matters
It would be easy to look at this construction programme today and read it as evidence that the young country was already stable and confident.
The historical context tells a more complicated story.
When Stadium Merdeka was being built in 1957, the Emergency was still ongoing.
The communist insurgency had posed a major security challenge since 1948, and although the Emergency formally ended in 1960, security concerns did not simply disappear.
Then came the question of Malaysia.
In 1961, Tunku Abdul Rahman proposed the formation of a larger federation involving Malaya, Singapore, Sabah, Sarawak and Brunei.
After negotiations and political upheaval, Malaysia was formed on September 16, 1963, with Malaya, Sabah, Sarawak and Singapore as its founding components.
The new federation was almost immediately confronted by Indonesia’s opposition.
Konfrontasi lasted from 1963 to 1966 and included armed incursions, bombings and other attacks.
At the same time, relations between Kuala Lumpur and Singapore deteriorated amid political and communal tensions.
Singapore left the federation on August 9, 1965.
Even then, the construction programme continued.
Masjid Negara was completed that August.
Subang Airport opened on August 30.
The country was dealing with confrontation, political tensions and an uncertain regional environment while continuing to build the infrastructure of a country that was supposed to grow and prosper.
That is what makes the buildings of this period so revealing.
They were not monuments built after the country had settled into a comfortable existence.
They were part of the process of trying to create that future.
An aerial view of the Parliament complex in Kuala Lumpur February 25, 2025. Parliament gave self-government a permanent home. — Picture by Sayuti Zainudin
An ambition in concrete
The buildings that rose after Merdeka can therefore be read as a kind of physical manifesto.
Stadium Merdeka made sovereignty visible.
The Federal Hotel projected a modern, outward-looking capital.
Parliament gave self-government a permanent home.
Dewan Bahasa dan Pustaka helped establish the institutions of the national language.
Muzium Negara provided a place to construct and preserve a national historical narrative.
Masjid Negara combined religious identity, local architectural traditions and modernity.
Klang Gates Dam provided the water needed for a growing capital.
Subang Airport connected the young country to the region and the wider world.
Their scale mattered. So did their speed.
So did the decision to make many of them unmistakably national in character.
They reflected a government that could not afford to wait for the country to become fully settled before beginning to build it.
In that sense, the architecture of the early post-Merdeka years was not simply a celebration of what Malaysia had already achieved.
It was a declaration of what it intended to become.
The country was modernising.
It was establishing its own institutions.
It was building infrastructure for economic growth.
It was creating national symbols for a population that remained diverse.
It was doing all of this while the political map around it was still shifting.
The eight years between 1957 and 1965 therefore produced an unusual landscape: one in which confidence and uncertainty existed side by side.
The country was young.
Its borders and political arrangements were still being tested.
Its security was fragile.
Its future was far from guaranteed.
Yet the concrete was already going up.
Perhaps that is the most enduring legacy of the buildings of the Merdeka era.
They were not evidence that the young country had everything figured out.
They were evidence that it had decided to build anyway and continue to do so.
Dewan Bahasa dan Pustaka moved into its own Kuala Lumpur headquarters as the institution tasked with developing and promoting the Malay language and literature. — Picture by Choo Choy May
Buildings that built the new nation
1957 — Stadium Merdeka
Completed in six months and opened on August 30, one day before independence. The next morning, Tunku Abdul Rahman proclaimed Malaya’s independence there.
1957 — Federal Hotel
Opened three days before Merdeka to accommodate foreign dignitaries and overseas guests attending the independence celebrations. It became a symbol of Kuala Lumpur’s emergence as a modern international capital.
1958 — Klang Gates Dam
Completed as the country’s first dam built for water supply, helping meet the needs of a growing Kuala Lumpur and Klang Valley.
Stadium Negara opened in 1962 as the country’s first indoor stadium, giving Kuala Lumpur another major venue for sports, exhibitions and public events. — Picture by Choo Choy May
1962 — Stadium Negara
Opened as Malaya’s first indoor stadium, providing a venue for sports, exhibitions and major public events.
1962 — Dewan Bahasa dan Pustaka
DBP moved into its own Kuala Lumpur headquarters as the institution tasked with developing and promoting the Malay language and literature.
1963 — Parliament
The new Parliament complex was completed in time for Malaysia’s formation. Its first sitting took place on September 16, 1963.
1963 — Muzium Negara
Opened on August 31, 1963, providing the new federation with a national institution to preserve and present its history and heritage.
1965 — Masjid Negara
Completed in August 1965. Its distinctive umbrella-shaped roof combined modern construction with local and Malay architectural influences.
1965 — Subang Airport
Opened on August 30, 1965, with what was then South-east Asia’s longest runway, connecting the young country to the wider region and world.
1965–66 — Dewan Tunku Canselor
Built at Universiti Malaya from 1965 and opened in 1966, extending the early post-Merdeka nation-building project into higher education.
A view of Dewan Tunku Canselor at Universiti Malaya in Kuala Lumpur October 27, 2014. It was built at Universiti Malaya from 1965 and opened in 1966, extending the early post-Merdeka nation-building project into higher education. — Picture by Yusof Mat Isa

Title: Patriotism, national assets and vibrant performances to take centre stage at Dataran Putrajaya tomorrow
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR, Aug 30 — Ahead of tomorrow’s 69th National Day celebration, Dataran Putrajaya is fully prepared to stage a grand gathering of thousands of participants, a showcase of national assets, and vibrant performances designed to ignite the people’s patriotic spirit.
Carrying the theme “Malaysia Madani:
Kesejahteraan Dinikmati
”, this year’s celebration features a colourful lineup that not only uplifts the love for the country but also highlights the values of struggle and identity in celebrating independence.
His Majesty Sultan Ibrahim, King of Malaysia, and Her Majesty Raja Zarith Sofiah, Queen of Malaysia, are scheduled to grace the celebration, which will also be attended by Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim and members of the Cabinet.
The event, scheduled to begin at 8am, involves 10,819 parade participants across 76 contingents, 22 marching bands, 11 float vehicles, 328 land, naval, and air assets, 112 working animals, and 22 electric vehicle (EV) assets.
Inspector General of Police Commissioner Datuk Seri Mohd Yusri Hassan Basri during the full rehearsal for the 69th National Day parade themed ‘Malaysia Madani: Kesejahteraan Dinikmati’ at Dataran Putrajaya August 29, 2026. — Bernama pic
The programme spans statehood, well-being, public order, and national security components, followed by an airshow and a special performance titled “
Rentak Madani, Paluan Tradisi
”.
Opening the event, the “Gema Inovasi Madani” performance — coordinated by the National Department for Culture and Arts under the Ministry of Tourism, Arts and Culture — will feature a fusion of traditional heritage percussion and innovation that elevates the spirit of togetherness.
Utilising 150 musical instruments and 700 traditional and innovative kompang (frame drums), the opening performance showcases a diversity of percussion instruments representing Malaysia’s main ethnic groups as symbols of well-being, harmony, goodwill, and loyalty.
The performance also serves as a manifestation of the Madani spirit in uplifting cultural heritage, innovation, unity, and national identity through creative approaches that connect traditional elements with modern renewal.
The statehood component features, among others, a large Jalur Gemilang-bearing contingent accompanied by the army, navy, and air force cadet officers from the National Resilience Leadership Academy, National Defence University of Malaysia (UPNM), alongside a National Service Training Programme (PLKN) contingent.
Communications Minister Datuk Seri Fahmi Fadzil inspects machinery showcased to the public as part of the Malaysian Armed Forces’ (MAF) asset participation in the 2026 National Day parade at Dataran Putrajaya August 29, 2026. — Bernama pic
Also participating is the sports well-being component, featuring national athletes and medalists from the Glasgow 2026 Commonwealth Games, carrying the spirit of Malaysian excellence onto the national and international stage.
The public well-being and economy component brings together a coalition of service providers and private sector entities, including Munchy’s Malaysia, ZUS Coffee, Siti Khadijah Apparel Sdn Bhd, the Malaysian Security Industry Association, MR. D.I.Y Group (M) Berhad, Angkatan Koperasi Kebangsaan Malaysia Berhad, and Carsome Sdn Bhd.
For the public order component, participating agencies include the Malaysia Civil Defence Force, the Road Transport Department, and the Malaysian Fire and Rescue Department, highlighting their roles in safeguarding the security and well-being of the people.
Also joining the parade is the Johor Military Force, the oldest military unit in Malaysia, which plays a role in defending the sovereignty and security of the Johor Royal Institution.
Meanwhile, floats for the Visit Malaysia Year 2026-2027 campaign will showcase state tourism icons, flora and fauna, traditional attire, and traditional musical instruments from Malaysia’s diverse communities.
The participation of airline strategic partners — Malaysia Airlines, AirAsia, Batik Air, and Air Borneo — will further enliven the procession, while national animation leader Les’ Copaque will feature popular characters Upin and Ipin as animation icons to enhance the celebration’s appeal among the younger generation and families.
A glimpse of the performances presented to visitors during the full parade rehearsal for the 2026 National Day celebrations at Dataran Putrajaya August 29, 2026. — Bernama pic
The National Day parade is also accompanied by the energetic actions of a human graphics performance bringing together 1,500 students from 36 schools in Selangor, displaying moving formations synchronised to music with visual changes in every segment.
The climax of the event is graced by an air show featuring the Royal Malaysian Air Force fighter jets slicing through the skies above the nation’s administrative center, capping off a display of the nation’s defence capabilities and assets before thousands of spectators.
The National and Malaysia Day 2026 theme song titled
Aku Berjanji
, composed and performed by renowned singer Faizal Tahir, will inject spirit and appreciation for the meaning of love for the country as the celebration concludes at approximately 10:00 am.
Yesterday, Communications Minister and Chairman of the Main Committee for the National Day and Malaysia Day (HKHM) 2026 Celebrations, Datuk Seri Fahmi Fadzil, advised visitors attending Dataran Putrajaya to wear N95 face masks to protect themselves from the current haze, a step aligned with Ministry of Health advice, particularly for high-risk individuals.
The HKHM 2026 organisers have also taken the approach of providing N95 face masks to over 10,000 participants of the 2026 National Day to ensure their health remains in optimal condition.
Meanwhile, the Ministry of Home Affairs via a Facebook infographic advised the public to plan their travel and utilise public transport due to the full closure of Putrajaya’s Core Island area, which begins on August 30 at 5am until August 31 at 6pm.
The road closures involve five main bridges — Seri Wawasan Bridge, Seri Saujana Bridge, Seri Gemilang Bridge, Putra Bridge, and Seri Ehsan Bridge — alongside several routes surrounding the central Putrajaya area. — Bernama

Title: Fashion designer Rizalman says adopted son stable, treated for liver injury after being dragged by lorry
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR, Aug 30 — Fashion designer Datuk Rizalman Ibrahim says his adopted son, Umar Nail, is in stable condition but remains under close medical observation following internal injuries sustained in a road accident.
He said doctors are focusing on treating Umar’s liver injury, which is currently the main concern, according to
Harian Metro
.
Rizalman said, “Alhamdulillah, as of now, Umar is stable,” adding that his son “is still under close monitoring by the medical team, particularly for injuries to his internal organs, namely the liver.”
He said he accepts the ordeal as a test for his family and places full trust in God’s will.
Rizalman said he continues to pray for Umar’s strength and recovery as treatment progresses.
He expressed gratitude to family members, friends, social media followers, media practitioners and hospital staff for their continuous support during this difficult period.
He said every prayer and message of encouragement has been a source of strength for the family.
Rizalman urged the public to continue praying for Umar’s healing and for his treatment process to be eased.
He also shared a series of Instagram Story posts describing how the accident occurred.
He said Umar had stepped out briefly after helping him cut lopes and was walking along the pedestrian path at Wangsa Walk when he and an ice delivery lorry “collided from behind.”
He said Umar fell under the lorry and was dragged for several seconds, resulting in complications to his internal organs.
He added that members of the public at the scene immediately came forward to help.

Title: ‘We have one homeland, Malaysia’: Anwar urges Malaysians to keep the spirit of independence alive
Article:
PUTRAJAYA, Aug 30 — The spirit of independence must continue to be nurtured in the hearts and minds of every Malaysian, with all communities united to build the nation, defend their rights and uphold justice, said Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim.
He said independence was not merely about systems or the nation itself, but, more importantly, about ensuring every Malaysian possessed a truly independent spirit.
“This is the greatest obstacle and challenge. That is why, to rebuild from the ruins, we must instil the spirit of independence in our hearts and minds. Therefore, we must unite.
“Who must unite? Our forefathers said it was not about uniting by race, district or region, but every single generation. This means every citizen — Malays and Bumiputera as the core, all communities must continue to unite and play their part in defending rights and upholding justice,” he said when delivering his National Day address at the Putrajaya International Convention Centre (PICC) here today.
Also present were Deputy Prime Minister Datuk Seri Dr Ahmad Zahid Hamidi, Communications Minister Datuk Seri Fahmi Fadzil and Chief Secretary to the Government Tan Sri Shamsul Azri Abu Bakar.
The Prime Minister said the spirit of independence must be translated into efforts to build a Malaysia Madani, drawing inspiration from the courage of past freedom fighters including Hang Tuah, Tok Janggut, Mat Kilau, Rosli Dhobi, Rentap, Mat Salleh and Antanom.
“Our nation’s forefathers faced adversity with courage and called on the people to unite, reach consensus, uphold their trust and the promises of the Proclamation of Independence, and rebuild after the fall of Melaka,” he said.
Anwar said Malaysia should be grateful that despite various problems, challenges and ups and downs, the country has remained one of the more peaceful nations, united by a shared sense of humanity across differences in race, religion and background.
He said Malaysia had also demonstrated to the world that the strength of unity could ensure the nation’s survival, particularly after independence in 1957, when some questioned whether Malaya could endure and bring together the strength of all communities.
“At the time of Merdeka in 1957, if we examine foreign media coverage, they did not believe Malaya could survive and harness the strength of all communities, given how many countries in Asia, Africa and the Americas had fallen apart.
“But we proved that we could endure. It is not that we had no tragic periods or tragedies, but we endured. With the great vision of the leaders and statesmen of that time, together with the great figures of Malaysia, what was once one strength — Malaya — is now three: Malaya, Sabah and Sarawak,” he said.
Anwar said Malaysia had continued to record several achievements in recent times, reflecting the country’s ability to defy the odds and overcome various challenges.
“Amid an uncertain geopolitical landscape, our GDP (gross domestic product) continues to grow. Alhamdulillah, Malaysia’s GDP grew by six per cent in the second quarter of 2026.
“Approved investments and total trade reached their highest levels since 1957 and 1963; Malaysia’s competitiveness climbed to 15th place in 2026, while our currency, the ringgit, emerged as Asia’s best-performing currency in 2025,” he said.
The Prime Minister said these achievements had not been realised overnight, but were the result of efforts and contributions built up since the country gained independence.
He said the Madani Government had chosen the more difficult path of strengthening the country’s fundamentals by improving governance, restoring fiscal discipline, closing loopholes and rebuilding confidence in Malaysia.
Anwar therefore urged Malaysians to remain united in developing the country, regardless of their backgrounds.
“Fellow Malaysians, rise, close ranks, strengthen our consensus, and unite our energy and efforts. We have one homeland, Malaysia.
“We have inherited the history of one Malaysian nation, and it is our responsibility to secure a great future. A Malaysia that is agile. A Malaysia that is stronger. A Malaysia whose standing can be elevated to glorious heights. This is our resolve as we celebrate our Independence Day,” he added. — Bernama

Title: AI for the People participants must complete six modules to receive free AI tools
Article:
PUTRAJAYA, Aug 30  — Participants in the AI for the People (AI Untuk Rakyat) programme must complete and pass six designated modules to qualify for a free three-month subscription to selected artificial intelligence (AI) applications and software.
The programme, which targets 100,000 Malaysians aged between 18 and 30 until 2027, will commence today in phases through the Rakyat Digital portal at rakyatdigital.gov.my, where interested youths can register.
In a statement today, the Digital Ministry said the six modules are AI Nation 2030: The Madani Approach, CYBERSAFE for the People, Generative AI, AI Security, Agentic AI for All and Cloud for the People.
“Participants who successfully complete and pass all the designated course modules will enjoy a free three-month subscription to various selected AI applications and software.
“For a start, eligible participants will be given special access to AI tools from local and international technology providers, namely YTL AI Labs — IlmuChat, Alibaba — Wonderclip and MuleRun, and Google — Gemini Enterprise,” it said.
The ministry said various other AI software and tools from technology companies would be added in phases to further enrich the learning experience.
It said the initiative would give youths opportunities to explore advanced technology practically, helping to enhance their creativity, productivity and digital skills.
“This initiative reflects the government’s commitment to ensuring that advancements in AI technology can be more widely utilised by the people, especially the youth, in line with Malaysia’s aspiration to develop an inclusive AI Nation by 2030, aligned with the Malaysia Digital 2030 aspirations,” it said.
The AI for the People programme was announced by Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim today as one of six initiatives aimed at opening up more digital opportunities for Malaysian youths, in conjunction with the 2026 National Day Premier Address at the Putrajaya International Convention Centre here.
Rakyat Digital is the national digital learning portal, an initiative of the Digital Ministry spearheaded by MyDIGITAL Corporation.
Meanwhile, Digital Ministry secretary-general Datuk Fabian Bigar said the AI for the People programme was an important step towards ensuring youths not only understood AI technology but also had access to AI tools that could be used for learning, creativity and productivity.
“Through this initiative, we want to ensure the benefits of AI can be felt more widely and inclusively, in line with the government’s aspiration to build a literate society ready to face the digital future,” he said. — Bernama

Title: Families of three missing Malaysians in Nepal hope for good news on their safety
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR, Aug 30 — The families and friends of three Malaysian climbers reported missing following a flash flood and landslide in the Nepal-Tibet border area last Wednesday are still hoping for good news regarding their safety.
The three climbers are Muhammad Muhaimin Azhad Noor Hadi, 27, Muhammad Adib Haikal Awang Mansor, 27, and Muhammad Zaki Othman, 29, who were reported uncontactable while undertaking a climbing activity in the Langtang Valley.
In a post on the Threads app, a friend of the three climbers appealed to the public to continue praying for their safety.
According to a post by user emyliatahar, the last message from the group was received at 10.42 am (Malaysia time) on the day of the incident, August 26, with their last location detected around the Bhote Koshi area.
“We have reported the disappearance of the three of them to the Malaysian Embassy in Nepal as well as Wisma Putra to enable follow-up action and rescue operations to be carried out,” she said.
Muhammad Muhaimin is from Gelugor, Penang, Muhammad Zaki from Kubang Semang, Bukit Mertajam, while Muhammad Adib Haikal is from Kulim, Kedah.
In another post on Threads, user myanaimah requested prayers from the public that her brother-in-law, Muhammad Adib Haikal, and his two friends are safe.
Meanwhile, Wisma Putra today held a special briefing session with the next-of-kin and family members to convey the latest updates regarding the case.
Family members have also been asked to be prepared to undergo deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) testing to assist in the identity verification process, following the discovery of unidentified remains in the disaster area. — Bernama

Title: Fahmi: 15 govt hospitals among early recipients of RM1b allocation to boost digital access and electronic medical record rollout
Article:
PUTRAJAYA, Aug 30 — A total of 15 government hospitals are among the initial group that will benefit from an allocation of RM1 billion to strengthen the digital efficiency of the public health sector, said Communications Minister Datuk Seri Fahmi Fadzil.
Fahmi, who is also the Madani Government spokesperson, said the allocation, which was increased from RM650 million as previously announced, would accelerate the implementation of the Electronic Medical Record (EMR) system as well as the provision of Internet access including public WiFi at health clinics and government hospitals.
“I will hold a discussion, initially 15 hospitals are expected to be completed but I will ask that this figure be increased further and from 2,000 health clinics, we will try to increase the number that can be managed for this year.
“This increase in allocation is aimed at accelerating efforts for digital access at health clinics and government hospitals as well as the e-medical record programme that we have implemented through the collaboration of MCMC (Malaysian Communications and Multimedia Commission) and the Ministry of Health,” he said.
He said this when met by reporters after the Prime Minister’s National Day Address at Putrajaya International Convention Centre (PICC), here today.
He said the pilot implementation of the EMR system at the Padang Besar Health Clinic had enabled doctors to access patient information electronically without having to refer to physical documents, thus saving time for those seeking treatment.
Meanwhile, Fahmi said the Ministry of Communications would help ensure that Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim’s message on various government assistance and successes was effectively conveyed to people.
He said further information on the offer of free subscription to artificial intelligence (AI) applications for 100,000 young people aged 18-30 years if they participate in the AI for the People programme, will be announced later.
Earlier, when delivering the Prime Minister’s Address on National Day, Anwar announced six major initiatives, including an allocation of RM1 billion to speed up treatment and reduce waiting times through the EMR system.
In addition, he also announced that the government agreed to restore the basic eligibility of the Budi Madani RON95 (BUDI95) Programme from 200 litres to 300 litres per month, BUDI Diesel from 300 litres to 400 litres per month, increase the e-Invoice exemption threshold from RM1 million to RM3 million per year, as well as free AI subscriptions to young people.
Anwar said the allocation for the maintenance of all types of schools for 2027 would be increased by 50 per cent, from RM1 billion to RM1.5 billion, introduce a RM200 million Madani Sejahtera Grant, to help hawkers, night market traders and mothers who trade from home, while micro-financing facilities will be increased by RM1 billion, bringing the total fund for 2026 to RM6 billion. — Bernama

Title: Family of missing Malaysian in Nepal urges govt to bring all victims home
Article:
PUTRAJAYA, Aug 30 — After nearly five days of anxious waiting, the family of N. Kalaiselvi, 65, who remains uncontactable in Nepal, is urging the government to bring the missing Malaysians home, regardless of their condition.
Her daughter, Kritikaa Joyce De Brito, said the family appreciated the Malaysian government’s efforts to coordinate the search and rescue mission, but acknowledged that their hopes were fading after nearly five days without contact.
She said that even if rescue teams successfully reached the affected area, the chances of finding the missing Malaysians alive could be slim given the conditions there.
“Even if they are found, they might be stranded in the forest or buried under eight feet of mud. The chances of survival are very slim.
“Therefore, our request is to bring them home. Regardless of the circumstances, whether they are still alive or not, we want them returned to us in Malaysia,” she told Bernama after attending a closed-door briefing for next of kin at Wisma Putra here today.
Kalaiselvi was among 27 Malaysians who travelled to Mount Kailash in Tibet, China, to perform religious ceremonies in a group managed by a local travel agency, before losing contact following flash floods and landslides in Rasuwa District last Wednesday.
Kritikaa said all family members present at today’s briefing agreed that the ministry should channel official updates and verified information directly to the next of kin.
She said the move was intended to curb speculation and the spread of false information that could further distress the victims’ families.
“For now, the ministry is being very careful with what is released to the public. We understand this because we want to avoid any speculation,” she said.
Earlier, Wisma Putra confirmed that 72 Malaysians in Darchen, China, were safe and receiving consular assistance, while another 55 remained uncontactable at the Nepal border. — Bernama

Title: Anwar announces six immediate measures to ease cost‑of‑living pressures
Article:
PUTRAJAYA, Aug 30 — Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim today announced six immediate measures for the people covering fuel subsidies, school maintenance, artificial intelligence (AI), healthcare digitalisation, e-Invoicing and microfinancing, which will take effect on September 1.
He said all the measures were part of the government’s efforts to address the people’s concerns, particularly those related to the cost of living and pressures of daily life.
“Although various measures have been implemented, I, the Deputy Prime Minister and the Cabinet have never assumed that we have solved all the problems, and this is not a curtain to conceal the people’s concerns. I understand that the people are still struggling with the cost of living.
“Therefore, on the eve of National Day, I have had to make efforts, seek solutions and take steps to announce something that can provide temporary relief... for schoolchildren, youths, housewives and mothers,” Anwar said when delivering the 2026 National Day Prime Minister’s Address at the Putrajaya International Convention Centre (PICC) here today.
Also present were Deputy Prime Minister Datuk Seri Dr Ahmad Zahid Hamidi, Communications Minister Datuk Seri Fahmi Fadzil, Cabinet ministers and Chief Secretary to the Government Tan Sri Shamsul Azri Abu Bakar.
Through the first measure, the Prime Minister said the government had agreed to restore the basic eligibility for the Budi Madani RON95 (BUDI95) programme from 200 litres to 300 litres per month, enabling more than 16 million users to enjoy subsidised RON95.
At the same time, he said more than half a million eligible owners of diesel-powered pickup trucks and four-wheel-drive vehicles would enjoy Budi Diesel of up to 400 litres per month.
He also announced that the allocation for the maintenance of all types of schools for 2027 would be increased by 50 per cent from RM1 billion to RM1.5 billion, covering all streams including national schools, Chinese and Tamil national-type schools, religious schools, tahfiz and pondok schools, as well as special education.
Anwar, who is also Finance Minister, said he had also instructed the Education Ministry to mobilise efforts at district level to scrutinise infrastructure repair applications so that maintenance work could begin as early as January 2027.
The third measure involves the AI for the People programme, which is open to Malaysian youths aged 18 to 30, with 100,000 youths who complete the prescribed modules to receive free subscriptions to AI applications for three months, including IlmuChat, Gemini Enterprise, Wonderclip and MuleRun.
For the fourth measure, the Prime Minister said the Malaysian Communications and Multimedia Commission (MCMC) would provide RM1 billion to strengthen the digital efficiency of the public healthcare sector, including the implementation of the Electronic Medical Records (EMR) system and Internet connectivity at 150 hospitals and more than 2,000 public health clinics.
“The government has also agreed to raise the e-Invoice exemption threshold from RM1 million to RM3 million annually, thereby exempting businesses with annual sales not exceeding RM3 million from the obligation to implement it,” he said.
In addition, microfinancing facilities would be increased by RM1 billion, bringing the total funding for 2026 from RM5 billion to RM6 billion.
Anwar said the government would also introduce the RM200 million Geran Sejahtera Madani to assist hawkers, small traders, night market traders and mothers running businesses from home.
“This is the spirit of our unity. Hopefully, all six measures can be implemented because they stem from one clear principle, namely that economic growth must be returned to the people,” Anwar said.
Meanwhile, in a Facebook post, Anwar said further announcements would be made during the Malaysia Day celebrations in Sarawak, as well as through the tabling of Budget 2027.
“Hopefully, these measures will, to some extent, ease the burden on the people and give real meaning to this year’s National Day celebrations,” he said.
The Prime Minister said he and the entire Madani Government team would continue to listen to the voices and concerns of the people and work hard to ensure that every achievement of the country was translated into greater benefits for the people and a more prosperous and dignified life. — Bernama

Title: Public urged to plan journey, arrive early amid National Day road closures in Putrajaya
Article:
PUTRAJAYA, Aug 30 — Members of the public planning to attend the 2026 National Day celebration at Dataran Putrajaya, here, tomorrow, are advised to plan their journey and arrive early, following the closure of several major roads around the government administrative centre.
Based on an infographic posted on the Merdeka360 Facebook page, the closures involve Putrajaya’s Core Island and several roads, from 5 am today until 6 pm tomorrow, to facilitate traffic flow in conjunction with the celebration.
